projects.title: Radish Salinity Experiment
projects.subtitle: Experimental exemplar emphasising treatment assignment, experimental units and pseudoreplication
projects.disclaimer: The three cited publications are real and independently checked. All procedures, data and results in this example are synthetic and do not document a conducted experiment. This 72-hour radicle-length example is separate from the Studio's Day 7 shoot-length response illustrations.
projects.rq: Under standardised germination conditions, how does mean radicle length among germinated radish (Raphanus sativus) seeds after 72 hours differ across dishes independently assigned to 0, 50, or 100 mM NaCl?

stages.title: Find a research interest
stages.where: The student begins with a broad interest in how environmental stress changes plant growth.
stages.changed: The idea moves from “plants and the environment” to several possible observable questions.
reasoning: Choose an area that is genuinely interesting.
Ask what could be observed or measured safely in a school setting.
Generate several possibilities before committing to one.
stages.decision: Retain salinity stress as one candidate. Preparing dilute NaCl solutions and handling germinating seeds may be feasible in a supervised school laboratory, subject to the setting's safety review.
stages.rejected: A project on road-salt effects in local soil was rejected because collecting representative field soil and controlling other environmental variables would make the first experiment harder to interpret.

notebook.phenomenon: Early seedling growth may change under salt stress
notebook.contextPop: Fast-germinating seeds under controlled classroom/laboratory conditions

stages.forward: This choice makes a short controlled plant experiment possible, but the exact species, salt levels, outcome, and unit are still undecided.
compare: What topic could you observe or measure with evidence you can actually access?
What tempting idea would become too large or poorly controlled for your timeline?

stages.title: Narrow the topic and test feasibility
stages.where: The student now needs one organism, one stressor, one developmental window, and a realistic outcome.
stages.changed: The topic becomes radish seed germination and early radicle growth under sodium chloride exposure.
reasoning: Radish seeds germinate quickly enough for a short instructional project.
Sodium chloride concentration can be prepared as explicit treatment levels.
Radicle length can be measured directly in millimetres.
Early growth is a narrower outcome than whole-plant fitness or crop yield.
stages.decision: Use radish (Raphanus sativus), NaCl treatments, and a 72-hour early-growth window.
stages.rejected: Long-term biomass and flowering outcomes were rejected because the course timeline and environmental control would be much more demanding.

notebook.scope: Early radicle growth over 72 hours; not whole-plant fitness, yield, or long-term salt tolerance
notebook.feasibility: A real project would need confirmed access to radish seeds, dishes, correctly prepared NaCl solutions, a suitable measurement scale and a supervised germination location.

stages.forward: The literature scan now needs terminology around salinity, germination, radicle growth, NaCl, and Raphanus sativus.
compare: Which part of your broad topic can one project answer well?
What outcome can you define and observe without pretending it represents a broader construct?

stages.title: Explore the research landscape
stages.where: The student performs a preliminary background scan before finalizing the question.
stages.changed: The student learns that salinity can influence plant growth through osmotic and ionic stress and that radish germination/radicle growth has been studied under saline conditions.
reasoning: Munns and Tester (2008) offer background on osmotic and ionic responses, without establishing the effect size under this proposed radish protocol.
Munns and Gilliham (2015) support the bounded background claim that salinity can constrain plant growth and yield.
Toscano et al. (2025) describe how radish germination and radicle development varied across tested temperatures and saline water potentials. Their methods differ from this teaching illustration.
The scan does not justify claiming that no one has studied radish and salinity.
stages.decision: Use the existing literature to support a local replication/extension teaching study, not a novelty claim.
stages.rejected: The statement “no research exists on salt and radish growth” is rejected because the preliminary search directly found relevant research.

notebook.known: Salinity can constrain plant growth, and radish early growth has been evaluated under saline germination conditions.
notebook.uncertain: The exact response of this seed batch under this classroom protocol and selected NaCl concentrations is not known in advance.

stages.forward: The research question can now specify assigned NaCl concentration, radish seeds, a 72-hour outcome, and a causal experimental structure.
compare: Did your background scan change the language you use for the topic?
Are you using a real rationale such as replication or extension instead of inventing a gap?

stages.title: Write and refine the research question
stages.where: The student converts the narrowed topic into one answerable causal question.
stages.changed: The question shifts from “Does salt affect plants?” to a bounded experimental question with treatment levels, outcome, organism, and timing.
reasoning: Assigning NaCl at the dish level permits an experimental comparison. Radicle length among germinated seeds requires additional care because germination occurs after treatment assignment.
The outcome must be defined at the level used for analysis.
The unit of treatment assignment will later determine the true n.
stages.decision: Under standardised germination conditions, how does mean radicle length among germinated radish (Raphanus sativus) seeds after 72 hours differ across dishes independently assigned to 0, 50, or 100 mM NaCl?
stages.rejected: “How does salt affect radish?” is rejected because neither salt exposure nor the outcome is defined precisely.

notebook.finalRQ: Under standardised germination conditions, how does mean radicle length among germinated radish (Raphanus sativus) seeds after 72 hours differ across dishes independently assigned to 0, 50, or 100 mM NaCl?
notebook.rqJustification: A short nonhuman experiment can assign NaCl concentration, standardise germination conditions, and measure radicle length within the course timeline.

stages.forward: The exact question determines the literature concepts, experimental treatment levels, outcome measurement, and later statistical structure.
compare: Does every noun in your question have a clear meaning in the planned study?
Does your wording imply causation, and does your actual design justify that wording?

stages.title: Build a systematic search strategy
stages.where: The student now documents how relevant literature will be located.
stages.changed: The search moves from one broad phrase to concept blocks with synonyms.
reasoning: Use a species block: radish OR Raphanus sativus.
Use a stress block: salinity OR salt stress OR sodium chloride OR NaCl.
Use an outcome block: germination OR radicle OR root growth OR seedling growth.
Record the database/search system, date, exact string, and filters.
stages.decision: Use multiple documented searches rather than treating one query as exhaustive.
stages.rejected: Searching only “salt plant experiment” is rejected because it is too broad and poorly reproducible.

notebook.searchBlock2: salinity OR "salt stress" OR "sodium chloride" OR NaCl
notebook.searchBlock3: germination OR radicle OR "root growth" OR "seedling growth"
notebook.searchStrings: ("Raphanus sativus" OR radish) AND (salinity OR "salt stress" OR NaCl) AND (germination OR radicle OR "seedling growth")

stages.forward: The search records will support transparent source selection and prevent an exaggerated gap statement later.
compare: What are the 2–3 concept blocks in your question?
What synonyms would researchers use that a beginner might not think of immediately?

stages.title: Evaluate, read, and extract sources
stages.where: The student turns relevant papers into comparable evidence records.
stages.changed: The student stops saving papers as isolated PDFs and records design, scope, findings, and limitations.
reasoning: Bibliographic verification is separate from judging methodological quality.
Broad reviews explain mechanisms but do not provide the exact classroom effect.
The radish study is directly relevant to species and early growth, while its conditions differ from this exemplar.
stages.decision: Keep three verified sources as background/example records, while continuing the real search in a real project.
stages.rejected: Treating every peer-reviewed source as equally strong or directly comparable is rejected.

notebook.sourceRecords: The three references E-S01, E-S02 and E-S03 have been checked against publisher and scholarly records. Their methods and findings must still be evaluated for the claim being made.
notebook.screeningLogic: Include sources that inform salinity mechanisms, radish germination, or early radicle growth; record differences in treatment and measurement.

stages.forward: The extracted records now make cross-study synthesis possible instead of producing an annotated bibliography.
compare: Can you tell what each source measured and what claim it can actually support?
Which source is background, which is closest to your question, and what still differs?

stages.title: Synthesize the literature and justify the study
stages.where: The student compares sources and chooses a defensible rationale.
stages.changed: The rationale changes from searching for novelty to a local replication/extension.
reasoning: Across the sources, salinity is a biologically plausible constraint on plant growth.
Radish early growth is responsive to saline conditions, but protocols and treatment scales vary.
A classroom experiment can reproduce the general phenomenon under a simpler protocol without claiming to discover a global gap.
stages.decision: Frame the proposed classroom protocol as a local extension of established salinity research, without suggesting it replicates a published method exactly.
stages.rejected: “No one has studied this” is explicitly rejected.

notebook.theme1: Salinity can constrain plant growth through osmotic/ionic stress mechanisms.
notebook.theme2: Radish germination and radicle growth vary with saline germination conditions.
notebook.tensions: Published protocols differ in temperature, water potential or NaCl treatment, outcomes, and duration.
notebook.gapStatement: This project is a local replication/extension of established salinity-growth research using a defined classroom protocol; it does not claim a global literature gap.

stages.forward: Because the rationale is replication/extension, the Discussion later should compare the direction of the synthetic teaching result with prior work without claiming novelty.
compare: What do several sources collectively support?
Would replication, extension, inconsistency, method comparison, or local relevance be more defensible than claiming a gap?

stages.title: Write the literature review
stages.where: The student converts source records into a connected argument that leads to the study.
stages.changed: The prose shifts from paper-by-paper summaries to claims supported by multiple sources.
reasoning: The opening establishes the biological processes that make salinity worth examining.
The discussion narrows to radish germination and radicle development in the published study.
The rationale for a classroom extension follows from the proposed treatment levels and measurements, without imposing a fixed sequence of paragraphs.
stages.decision: Use synthesis language and preserve the boundary between broad salinity evidence and the exact classroom protocol.
stages.rejected: A sequence such as “Munns studied… Toscano studied…” is rejected because it does not explain relationships among the sources.

notebook.literatureReviewExcerpt: Salinity can constrain plant growth through osmotic and ionic stress, although tolerance depends on species, developmental stage, and environmental conditions (Munns & Tester, 2008; Munns & Gilliham, 2015). Species-relevant work also demonstrates that radish germination and early radicle growth respond to saline germination conditions (Toscano et al., 2025). These studies establish the biological plausibility of a salt-growth response while leaving the exact magnitude under any new classroom protocol to be measured directly.

stages.forward: The Method must now operationalize the causal question exactly as the literature review and RQ describe it.
compare: Does each paragraph make a claim about the literature rather than just name authors?
Does the final paragraph lead logically to your actual question?

stages.title: Choose the research design
stages.where: The student chooses the evidence structure that can answer the causal question.
stages.changed: The study is explicitly defined as a completely randomised nonhuman experiment.
reasoning: NaCl concentration will be assigned by the researcher.
Different dishes will receive one of three conditions.
Random assignment of dishes to conditions helps reduce systematic baseline differences.
The causal claim remains limited to the protocol, tested seed lot, and conditions.
stages.decision: Completely randomised experiment with 18 Petri dishes, 6 assigned to each NaCl level.
stages.rejected: An observational design is rejected because the project is able to assign the exposure directly.

notebook.designWhy: NaCl concentration is deliberately assigned to independent dishes, allowing a controlled treatment comparison.
notebook.comparisonStructure: 18 independent dishes; 6 dishes each at 0, 50, and 100 mM NaCl.
notebook.claimBoundary: Random assignment permits comparisons of NaCl conditions at the dish level under this protocol. The primary outcome is mean radicle length among seeds that germinated, which cannot isolate an effect on radicle elongation independently of treatment-related changes in germination.

stages.forward: The next stage must identify the experimental unit correctly. The number of seeds cannot automatically become the treatment n.
compare: Was your key exposure actually assigned?
What is the strongest claim your design can support before you know the result?

stages.title: Define hypotheses, variables, controls, and units
stages.where: The student translates the experimental question into exact roles and operational definitions.
stages.changed: The student discovers that the dish, not the individual seed, is the experimental unit because treatment is assigned to the whole dish.
reasoning: NaCl concentration is the manipulated independent variable.
The primary outcome is mean radicle length among germinated seeds at 72 hours within each dish, alongside the dish's germination proportion.
Five seeds inside one dish are subsamples sharing the same treatment environment.
The 0 mM condition is the control/reference condition.
standardising volume, seed batch, substrate, temperature range, timing, and measurement reduces alternative explanations.
stages.decision: analyse treatment replication at the dish level (n = 18 dishes), while retaining seed-level raw records as subsamples.
stages.rejected: n = 90 independent treatment replicates is rejected because 90 seeds are nested within only 18 independently treated dishes.

notebook.researchHyp: Higher assigned NaCl concentration will reduce mean radicle length per dish after 72 hours.
notebook.outcomeDV: Mean radicle length in millimetres among germinated seeds within each dish at 72 hours.
notebook.operationalDefs: Measure the radicle from the emergence point at the seed coat to the tip. Calculate one mean from germinated seeds in each dish; an ungerminated seed has no radicle-length measurement and is not coded as zero. A dish with no germinated seeds would have an undefined mean and requires a prespecified handling rule.
notebook.controlledConditions: Same seed lot, 5 seeds per dish, substrate, solution volume, temperature range, light exposure, incubation time, and measurement procedure.
notebook.experimentalUnit: Petri dish; seeds within a dish are subsamples.

stages.forward: Sampling, measurement and analysis must retain dish IDs and distinguish conditional radicle length from germination itself.
compare: What could independently receive a different treatment?
Are you counting repeated readings or subsamples as if they were independent experiments?

stages.title: Plan sampling, measurement, validity, and ethics
stages.where: The student decides what the sample represents and how measurements will be made consistently.
stages.changed: The project stops implying that one commercial seed packet represents all radish plants.
reasoning: The seed lot is a convenience biological sample.
generalisation should stay close to this seed batch and protocol.
Radicle length is measured in millimetres using the same image/ruler procedure and time point.
Nonhuman work avoids participant-consent issues, but ordinary lab safety and disposal rules still apply.
stages.decision: Use one accessible radish seed lot, 18 dishes, standardised measurement at 72 hours, and a bounded generalisation statement.
stages.rejected: “Random sample of all radish seeds” is rejected because the seeds come from one accessible commercial batch.

notebook.population: Radish seeds comparable to the tested commercial batch under similar early germination conditions.
notebook.sample: 90 seeds from one accessible commercial seed lot placed into 18 dishes.
notebook.samplingMethod: Convenience biological sample from one seed lot; treatment is randomised at the dish level.
notebook.sampleLimits: Results should not be generalised to all radish cultivars, field soils, or long-term plant performance.
notebook.instrument: standardised millimetre measurement from seed coat to radicle tip at 72 hours, using the same scale/procedure.
notebook.measureQuality: Same measurer/protocol and time point; coded dish images can reduce expectation effects during measurement.
notebook.ethicsIssues: No human participants. Use ordinary classroom laboratory safety for salt solutions, biological material, and disposal.
notebook.ethicsPlan: Seek teacher approval before any classroom laboratory work, label solutions clearly, and follow the school's handling and disposal requirements.

stages.forward: The written protocol must now specify exactly how dishes are assigned, prepared, measured, and converted into a dish-level analysis table.
compare: Who or what is actually sampled, and what broader group are you tempted to generalise to?
What evidence supports the interpretation of your measurement?

stages.title: Write the method and lock the data plan
stages.where: The student writes the protocol before seeing the final result and defines two linked data tables.
stages.changed: The vague instruction “measure growth” becomes an auditable sequence with raw seed-level records and a dish-level analysis file.
reasoning: Randomly assign 18 labelled dishes to three NaCl conditions.
Place five seeds in each dish and apply the same solution volume.
Incubate under the same conditions for 72 hours.
Record germination and radicle length for each seed.
Compute one mean radicle-length value per dish for the primary analysis.
Preserve seed_id and dish_id so subsamples remain linked.
stages.decision: Lock a protocol that treats the dish as the experimental unit and uses dish-level mean radicle length as the primary analysis outcome.
stages.rejected: A spreadsheet with one row per seed and no dish ID is rejected because it would invite pseudoreplication.

notebook.procedure: randomise 18 dishes to 0, 50, or 100 mM NaCl; place 5 seeds per dish; add equal solution volume; incubate 72 hours under standardised conditions; score germination and radicle length; preserve seed and dish IDs; summarise mean radicle length by dish.
notebook.replication: 18 independent dishes total, 6 per condition; 5 seed subsamples per dish.
notebook.rowUnit: Primary analysis table: one row = one dish. Raw table: one row = one seed linked to dish_id.
notebook.columns: dish_id, NaCl_mM, n_seeds, n_germinated, germination_proportion, mean_radicle_length_mm.
notebook.missingRule: For an ungerminated seed, radicle length is not applicable and remains blank while germination is coded 0. A dish with no germinated seeds has an undefined conditional mean; the protocol must set out how such dishes will be reported before data collection.
notebook.analysisIntent: Compare dish-level mean radicle length among germinated seeds across the three independently assigned NaCl groups, while reporting germination proportions separately.

stages.forward: Because the protocol is locked before final data, later exclusions or changes must be logged instead of silently adjusted to improve the result.
compare: Could another student run your procedure without inventing missing decisions?
What does one row represent, and does that match the independent unit?

stages.title: Collect, clean, visualise, and describe data
stages.where: The exemplar now introduces synthetic data solely to demonstrate the analysis workflow.
stages.changed: The project moves from planned variables to actual-looking records while preserving the dish as the analysis unit.
reasoning: The seed-level file keeps raw subsample information.
The dish-level file contains the independent units used in the primary analysis.
No dish-level value is missing in the synthetic dataset.
Mean dish-level radicle length declines across 0, 50, and 100 mM groups in the synthetic data.
Germination proportion is summarised secondarily without pretending seed rows are independent treatment replicates.
stages.decision: Use the dish-level dataset for treatment inference and retain the seed-level file for auditability.
stages.rejected: Running the primary group comparison on all seed rows as n = 90 is rejected.

notebook.rawLocation: Synthetic teaching files: SYNTHETIC_SEED_LEVEL_DATA.csv and SYNTHETIC_DISH_LEVEL_ANALYSIS_DATA.csv.
notebook.missingObserved: Ten synthetic seed records describe seeds that did not germinate and therefore have no radicle length. Every dish has at least three germinated seeds, so all 18 dish-level conditional means are defined.
notebook.descriptives: 0 mM: mean 34.70 mm, SD 1.21; 50 mM: mean 26.78 mm, SD 1.30; 100 mM: mean 16.57 mm, SD 1.13. Mean germination proportions are 1.00, 0.93, and 0.73.

stages.forward: The analysis compares independent dishes using an outcome conditional on germination. Differences in germination proportion must also inform interpretation.
compare: Is your analysis file using the same unit that your design identified as independent?
Do blanks mean missing, zero, not applicable, or something else?

stages.title: Choose and justify the data analysis
stages.where: The student chooses the analysis from the estimand, outcome type, and unit structure.
stages.changed: The analysis decision follows design structure instead of starting with a favourite test name.
reasoning: The treatment comparison concerns dish-level means computed only for seeds that germinated by 72 hours; germination is reported separately.
The outcome is numerical.
The treatment groups contain different independent dishes.
Welch ANOVA permits unequal group variances, although six dishes per group limit diagnostic certainty and warrant cautious inference.
A prespecified 0 vs 100 mM contrast communicates a directly interpretable raw difference in millimetres.
stages.decision: Primary analysis: Welch one-way ANOVA on the 18 dish means. Prespecified secondary contrast: Welch independent-groups comparison of 0 vs 100 mM dish means.
stages.rejected: An analysis with 90 independent seed observations is rejected because it violates the experimental-unit structure.

notebook.primaryEstimand: Differences among the assigned NaCl concentrations in mean dish-level radicle length among seeds that germinated by 72 hours.
notebook.analysisChoice: Welch one-way ANOVA for the three independent dish groups; prespecified 0 vs 100 mM Welch contrast for an interpretable raw difference.
notebook.assumptionChecks: Independent assignment at dish level; inspect group distributions and extreme dish values; numerical outcome measured on the same scale.
notebook.effectSizePlan: Report group means/SDs and the raw 0 vs 100 mM mean difference with 95% CI. millimetres are directly interpretable; do not use p as an effect size.

stages.forward: The Results must report the actual estimates and uncertainty without introducing a biological mechanism that was not directly measured.
compare: What exact quantity would answer your question even if you never calculated a p-value?
Are your groups independent, paired, repeated, or nested?

stages.title: Write the Results section
stages.where: The student converts the synthetic analysis output into neutral, traceable Results prose.
stages.changed: The student stops at what the data show and does not yet explain why salt changes growth.
reasoning: Report n at the dish level.
Report group means and SDs.
Report the Welch ANOVA statistic and degrees of freedom.
Report the prespecified raw difference and 95% CI.
Keep germination as a secondary descriptive result.
stages.decision: Write the Results around dish-level estimates and uncertainty.
stages.rejected: “Salt damaged the seedlings by disrupting water balance” is rejected from Results because mechanism was not measured and belongs, if used cautiously, in Discussion.

notebook.result1: Synthetic dish-level mean radicle length was 34.70 mm (SD 1.21) at 0 mM, 26.78 mm (SD 1.30) at 50 mM, and 16.57 mm (SD 1.13) at 100 mM. Welch ANOVA indicated a difference among condition means, F(2, 9.97) = 342.91, p < .001.
notebook.result2: The prespecified 0 vs 100 mM raw mean difference was 18.13 mm, 95% CI [16.63, 19.64]. Mean dish germination proportions were 1.00, 0.93, and 0.73 across increasing concentrations.
notebook.resultsDraft: In these synthetic data, the mean radicle length among germinated seeds is lower in dishes assigned higher NaCl concentrations. The Welch analysis compares 18 dish-level conditional means, and germination proportions are reported separately.

stages.forward: Discussion can now interpret the direction, compare it with the literature, and explain boundaries. It cannot erase that the data are synthetic teaching data.
compare: Can every number in your Results be traced to an output or table?
Have you accidentally explained a mechanism instead of reporting a finding?

stages.title: Write the Discussion and limitations
stages.where: The student interprets the synthetic result while separating observation, mechanism, and limitation.
stages.changed: The paper now answers the RQ and links the result to prior salinity literature without claiming that the teaching data prove a universal mechanism.
reasoning: The synthetic dish-level outcome among germinated seeds decreases in the higher-NaCl groups; the pattern is invented, not an observed treatment effect.
This direction is consistent with literature showing salinity can constrain plant growth and radicle development.
Osmotic/ionic stress is a plausible explanation from prior literature, but it was not directly measured here.
One seed lot, one short time point, simple laboratory conditions, and synthetic data sharply limit the claim.
stages.decision: Use a bounded causal interpretation for the specified experimental protocol, then explicitly state that the teaching data themselves are synthetic and cannot serve as empirical evidence.
stages.rejected: “Salt always prevents radish growth” is rejected as an unjustified universal conclusion.

notebook.directAnswer: The synthetic dish-level means among germinated seeds decrease across assigned 0, 50 and 100 mM NaCl conditions. Because germination differs across groups, these conditional length differences cannot isolate radicle elongation among all planted seeds.
notebook.interpret1: The direction is consistent with published salinity research, but the exemplar did not measure osmotic or ionic mechanisms directly.
notebook.alternatives: Seed-batch characteristics, small environmental differences among dishes, and measurement error could contribute to variation, although random assignment and standardisation are intended to reduce systematic bias.
notebook.limitations: One commercial seed lot, 18 dishes, a 72-hour window, simplified growing conditions, and wholly synthetic data limit the example. The mean radicle length includes only germinated seeds, whose composition may differ by assigned treatment.
notebook.implications: The workflow demonstrates how to align treatment assignment, experimental unit, analysis, and claim calibration. It is not evidence that students should cite as a biological finding.

stages.forward: The conclusion and abstract must preserve the same scope and synthetic-data disclaimer.
compare: Which explanation comes from your data and which comes from prior literature?
For every limitation, what specific claim becomes weaker?

stages.title: Write the conclusion, abstract, title, and keywords
stages.where: The student closes the paper only after the Method, Results, and Discussion are stable.
stages.changed: The abstract now contains the actual design and central synthetic result rather than vague promises.
reasoning: The title names the treatment, outcome, organism, and exemplar status.
The abstract states purpose, design, unit, result, and bounded conclusion.
The conclusion does not introduce new data or a new literature claim.
stages.decision: Make the synthetic instructional status impossible to miss.
stages.rejected: A title such as “The Effect of Salt on Plants” is rejected as vague and overbroad.

notebook.titleDraft: Synthetic Teaching Exemplar: Assigned Sodium Chloride Concentration and Early Radicle Growth in Radish Seeds
notebook.abstractDraft: This synthetic instructional exemplar follows a randomised experimental design with 18 Petri dishes independently assigned to 0, 50 or 100 mM NaCl, with five radish seeds nested within each dish. The primary outcome is mean radicle length among germinated seeds within each dish at 72 hours. In the synthetic data, the 18 dish-level means differ across groups, Welch F(2, 9.97) = 342.91, p < .001, and the 0 versus 100 mM mean difference is 18.13 mm, 95% CI [16.63, 19.64]. Because germination proportions vary by group, this conditional length outcome cannot distinguish germination from elongation differences among all planted seeds. The invented values illustrate experimental-unit reasoning and evidence-bounded reporting; they are not biological findings.
notebook.keywords: salinity; radish; Raphanus sativus; radicle growth; experimental design; synthetic teaching data

stages.forward: The final audit must now verify that citations are real, all numerical results trace to the synthetic files, and the wording never hides the exemplar status.
compare: If a reader saw only your abstract, could they tell what was done and what was found?
Does the title imply more causality or generality than the design supports?

stages.title: Citations, references, and final alignment audit
stages.where: The student checks the entire chain from interest to claim.
stages.changed: The final review catches alignment errors that ordinary grammar proofreading would miss.
reasoning: The research question asks about assigned NaCl concentration and dish-level mean radicle length.
The Method assigns treatment to dishes and preserves seeds as subsamples.
The analysis uses dish-level means rather than pretending 90 seeds are independent treatment replicates.
The analysis reports conditional radicle-length differences among germinated seeds, while germination proportions remain visible.
The Discussion and abstract retain the experimental scope and synthetic-data disclaimer.
All three bibliography records are real and verified; the synthetic data are never presented as published evidence.
stages.decision: Freeze the exemplar as a complete teaching chain, with its data, source records, analysis output, and paper stored together.
stages.rejected: A polished paper with a unit mismatch, invented DOI, or unsupported causal/generalisation claim is rejected even if its grammar is excellent.

notebook.citationAudit: E-S01, E-S02 and E-S03 correspond to independently checked publications. The exemplar's synthetic figures reconcile with the supplied dish-level analysis file; no measurements reflect a conducted classroom experiment.
notebook.finalEdits: Confirm synthetic-data labels, dish-level n = 18, exact Welch ANOVA values, APA references, and consistency of 0/50/100 mM treatment descriptions.

stages.forward: The research chain is complete. A real student project would now be submitted with its own raw evidence, audit trail, and teacher approval records.
compare: Can you trace every major claim backward to either data or a verified source?
If you changed one early decision, which later sections would also need revision?

Specify three aquaria and seven days, rather than implying a wider system was sampled.

Acknowledge the constructed time trend without calling it proof that temperature caused changes in oxygen.

In the abstract, identify three aquaria followed for seven school days and distinguish 21 aquarium-day observations from 21 independent aquaria.
Close with the actual descriptive contribution, noting that the invented values have no empirical standing.

notebook.title: Synthetic Descriptive Exemplar on Temperature and Dissolved Oxygen in Three Classroom Aquaria
notebook.abstractDraft: This synthetic teaching exemplar illustrates a descriptive monitoring design for water temperature and dissolved oxygen in three classroom aquaria over seven school days. The illustrative file contains one record per aquarium-day, yielding 21 repeated observations from three systems. Across the invented readings, water temperature averaged 23.93 °C and ranged from 22.5 to 25.7 °C. Dissolved oxygen averaged 7.60 mg/L, with recorded values from 6.85 to 8.19 mg/L. Aquarium-specific averages also differed, and each synthetic series showed higher temperatures and lower oxygen concentrations at the end of the seven-day period. The project demonstrates how to retain aquarium identifiers, report repeated measurements transparently and interpret descriptive trends cautiously. No interventions, organism outcomes or actual instrument logs are represented. These values were created for instruction and cannot establish water quality in any real school aquarium.
notebook.keywords: dissolved oxygen; water temperature; classroom aquaria; descriptive monitoring; synthetic data

projects.title: Reported Sleep and Biology Quiz Scores
projects.subtitle: Observational exemplar emphasizing confounding and noncausal claims
projects.rq: Among students in one synthetic biology-class sample, what is the association between reported weekday sleep duration and biology quiz score?
projects.disclaimer: The two cited sleep reviews are genuine scholarly publications. The 30 student records and their statistical association are invented teaching data, not observations of identifiable students or evidence of a real classroom effect.
projects.data_summary: 30 distinct synthetic student records. Sleep mean 6.98 hours and quiz-score mean 92.32; six scores reach 100. The constructed Pearson association is r = .7472, with a conventional two-sided p ≈ 2.10 × 10⁻⁶. No empirical or causal result is implied.

sources.citation: Dewald, J. F., Meijer, A. M., Oort, F. J., Kerkhof, G. A., & Bögels, S. M. (2010). The influence of sleep quality, sleep duration and sleepiness on school performance in children and adolescents: A meta-analytic review. Sleep Medicine Reviews, 14(3), 179–189. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.smrv.2009.10.004
sources.use: Meta-analysis of distinct sleep measures and school performance. Its pooled sleep-duration correlation was modest (r = .069), much smaller than the deliberately constructed exemplar's r = .7472.
sources.boundary: The pooled estimate combines heterogeneous published studies and cannot substantiate the fictional class's correlation or imply a causal effect.

sources.citation: Curcio, G., Ferrara, M., & De Gennaro, L. (2006). Sleep loss, learning capacity and academic performance. Sleep Medicine Reviews, 10(5), 323–337. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.smrv.2005.11.001
sources.use: Review of sleep loss, learning and academic performance across observational and manipulated-sleep research, providing contextual rather than sample-specific evidence.
sources.boundary: Designs and outcomes in this review differ from the invented single-quiz observational dataset. It does not verify the exemplar's effect size, survey procedure or causal mechanism.

Keep the intended inference modest, since sleep is a naturally varying experience rather than a treatment students can simply be assigned.
stages.decision: Retain the possible relationship between reported sleep and biology assessment performance as an observational topic to examine for feasibility.
stages.rejected: Asking whether more sleep makes students better at biology presumes causation before the design or evidence has been established.

stages.forward: The two available reviews can now be read for their designs and the specific associations they report.
compare: Would your search also retrieve studies with weak or null associations?
Can another student identify exactly where and how you searched?

stages.title: Evaluate, read, and extract sources
stages.where: The student evaluates two genuine review articles as sources for a bounded classroom rationale.
stages.changed: Source authority is considered alongside study design, construct definitions and limits on transfer to the example.
reasoning: Dewald et al. (2010) conducted separate meta-analyses of sleep quality, duration and sleepiness; their estimates should not be treated as interchangeable.
Curcio et al. (2006) discussed research on sleep loss, learning and performance, including both correlational and manipulated-sleep designs.
Neither paper reports results for the fictional biology quiz, and neither supplies a survey instrument or consent record for this exemplar.
stages.decision: Retain the reviews for background while documenting how their educational outcomes and sleep measures differ from the proposed class-level comparison.
stages.rejected: A citation to a well-known review does not independently validate an invented correlation or imply that all confounding has been addressed.

notebook.sourceExtraction: O-S01 is a meta-analytic review separating sleep measures and reporting a modest sleep-duration association with school performance. O-S02 reviews sleep loss, learning and educational performance across varied designs. Both are background sources, not classroom data.

stages.forward: The literature synthesis should explain what is plausible without making the invented result appear expected or independently corroborated.
compare: Does the research design in a source justify its particular inference?
Which variables and outcomes differ from those used in the teaching dataset?

stages.title: Synthesize the literature and justify the study
stages.where: The rationale connects a measurable classroom association to a wider but heterogeneous sleep literature.
stages.changed: An unsupported novelty claim is replaced by a local measurement and inferential demonstration.
reasoning: Published work provides reasons to investigate sleep-related variables and school performance, while reporting effect sizes that vary across constructs.
A short classroom study could illustrate how a measured predictor and a quiz score are linked, with appropriate ethical safeguards.
The synthetic data are deliberately constructed to provide a visible association, so they cannot independently replicate or extend a published empirical finding.
stages.decision: Frame the example as a demonstration of observational measurement, correlation and the boundaries of educational inference.
stages.rejected: The statement that researchers have not explored sleep and grades is contradicted by the two cited reviews.

notebook.rationale: An association-focused example can teach how to measure two variables, inspect a scatterplot and communicate uncertainty without converting correlation into causation.

stages.forward: The literature review can now develop the relationship between reported sleep constructs, performance and limits of comparison.
compare: What can a new sample contribute without claiming global novelty?
Is the stated gap demonstrated or merely asserted?

stages.title: Write the literature review
stages.where: The student assembles a short argument that leads from sleep research to the chosen observational question.
stages.changed: General instructions to synthesise sources become a specific comparison between review findings and the illustrative class variables.
reasoning: Introduce the distinction between sleep duration, sleep quality and sleepiness because these measures can show different associations with school performance.
Use the meta-analytic sleep-duration result to demonstrate why magnitudes cannot be assumed across settings and outcomes.
Explain how self-report and prior achievement could affect an apparent class-level relationship before posing the bounded question.
stages.decision: Write a background passage that supports studying the association while avoiding a prediction of the synthetic correlation's strength.
stages.rejected: Describing a synthetic r = .75 as confirmation of Dewald et al. (2010) would obscure that their pooled duration association was about r = .069.

notebook.literatureReviewPlan: Sleep research considers several related measures. In a meta-analysis of school-age samples, Dewald et al. (2010) found a modest pooled association between sleep duration and school performance, whereas Curcio et al. (2006) reviewed wider evidence on sleep loss and learning. The present instructional comparison uses reported weekday sleep and one biology quiz score, so its constructed figures must remain separate from these empirical sources.

stages.forward: The design now has to explain precisely what is measured and why no treatment effect can be inferred.
compare: Does the paragraph carry an idea across sources rather than merely listing their titles?
Can the reader tell which quantities are published evidence and which are fabricated for teaching?

stages.title: Choose the research design
stages.where: The research design is selected to estimate a relationship between existing reports and scores.
stages.changed: The project is explicitly observational and cross-sectional, with no random assignment of sleep duration.
reasoning: Each synthetic student row includes a reported sleep number and a quiz score, both referring to the same coded identifier.
The file does not record manipulation of sleep, repeated quiz measurements or time-ordered changes.
Even a large statistically significant correlation cannot separate the effect of sleep from prior achievement, study habits and other possible explanations.
stages.decision: Use a descriptive correlational design with one observation per student and Pearson correlation as a possible association estimate.
stages.rejected: Calling the two variables an experimental treatment and outcome would create an unsupported causal design.

notebook.claimBoundary: Estimate the association between reported sleep hours and quiz scores within the constructed sample; do not claim that increasing sleep would change scores or that the records represent all students.

stages.forward: The next decisions concern operational definitions, the score boundary and the level at which each measurement is recorded.
compare: Was the explanatory variable assigned or simply reported?
Can the chosen method identify a cause without additional evidence?

stages.title: Define constructs, variables, or evidence units
stages.where: The student translates the question into measured variables and a clearly identified record unit.
stages.changed: Sleep is identified as a self-reported predictor, while the quiz score remains an outcome whose scoring procedure would need documentation in real research.
reasoning: Each row represents one student ID with one reported weekday sleep-hours value, one weekly study-hours value and one quiz score.
The file does not identify the exact sleep survey question, reporting period, quiz rubric or administration date; these cannot be inferred from the numbers.
Six of the synthetic quiz values are 100, so the upper score boundary and overall distribution warrant inspection before interpreting Pearson correlation.
stages.decision: Describe the two central variables as measured numbers and retain weekly study hours as a possible accompanying predictor rather than a proven confounder.
stages.rejected: Calling sleep an assigned independent variable would misstate the design and obscure the meaning of the observed association.

notebook.predictor: reported_weekday_sleep_hours, one synthetic student-level self-report value in hours; original questionnaire wording unavailable.
notebook.outcome: biology_quiz_score, a synthetic numerical score ranging from 75.2 to 100.0; the original quiz scoring method is not documented.
notebook.unit: One student identifier, S01 through S30, per row. No repeated measurements are supplied.
notebook.confounders: weekly_study_hours appears in the CSV, but prior achievement, attendance, stress, family circumstances and other potentially relevant variables are unrecorded.

stages.forward: A genuine classroom study would need a documented sampling and consent process, valid measurement procedures and controlled access to educational records.
compare: What does the file actually reveal about the measurement process?
Does an observed extra variable necessarily explain the association?

stages.title: Plan sampling, measurement, validity, and ethics
stages.where: The student considers sampling, privacy and the power relationship involved in teacher-led educational research.
stages.changed: A fictional classroom sample becomes an explicit example for planning voluntary participation and safeguarding linked records.
reasoning: Thirty invented student IDs provide an illustration of a convenience class rather than an empirical sample with consent records.
A teacher's access to grades does not automatically authorise research use; recruitment and permission requirements depend on school and applicable ethics procedures.
Students may perceive pressure when a teacher requests sleep information or permission to use their quiz results, so an independent consent process and non-participation safeguards may be necessary.
stages.decision: For a real study, seek the required permissions and ethics review, define recruitment separately from grading, and minimise identifying information in the linked dataset.
stages.rejected: Treating automatically accessible grade records as anonymous research data would be misleading; coding alone does not guarantee anonymity.

notebook.sample: A fully synthetic 30-row file resembling one accessible biology class; no real participants were enrolled.
notebook.sampling: Illustrative convenience sampling only. A real analysed sample would depend on eligible students and voluntary consent, not simply class enrolment.
notebook.ethics: Plan school permission and applicable research ethics review before data access; use age-appropriate consent/assent and any required parental permission, with participation separated from grading. Protect the code key and explain withdrawal and re-identification limits.

stages.forward: The proposed measurement and data-processing rules should preserve the student-level linkage without exposing identities.
compare: Who controls permission to use students' grades, and who handles consent?
Would a student feel free to decline participation if their own teacher were recruiting?

stages.title: Write the method and lock the data plan
stages.where: The data plan specifies how student-level sleep, study-time and score values are linked.
stages.changed: A generic one-row-per-student instruction becomes an explicit four-column schema and a distinction between the synthetic file and a real protocol.
reasoning: Preserve the actual CSV headers student_id, reported_weekday_sleep_hours, weekly_study_hours and biology_quiz_score.
Check for duplicated identifiers, absent values and scores near the observed maximum before choosing how to display the data.
For real records, define the sleep reporting window, the quiz-score scale, access rights and procedures for handling missing responses before data collection.
stages.decision: Use one row per synthetic student and retain all four provided variables, while treating student_id as a record key rather than a numerical predictor.
stages.rejected: Interpreting a blank sleep response as zero hours or changing high quiz scores because they seem inconvenient would distort the records.

notebook.rowUnit: One synthetic student with one sleep report, one weekly study-hours value and one biology quiz score.
notebook.columns: student_id (record identifier); reported_weekday_sleep_hours (hours); weekly_study_hours (hours); biology_quiz_score (numerical score, observed range 75.2–100.0).

stages.forward: The analytical checks can now reproduce the association and examine the spread of each measure.
compare: Does the stored column name carry the unit or do you need an accompanying codebook?
How would you distinguish missing responses from real zeroes?

stages.title: Collect or organise evidence
stages.where: The analysis begins with an inspection of the 30 fabricated student records.
stages.changed: The dataset description includes the distributional context needed to interpret a correlation.
reasoning: All 30 student IDs are distinct and the four expected columns are present in the supplied synthetic CSV.
Reported weekday sleep values range from 4.8 to 9.2 hours, with a mean of 6.98 hours. Quiz scores range from 75.2 to 100.0, averaging 92.32.
Six scores equal 100.0, creating a visible upper-bound concentration; a scatterplot is needed to assess whether the positive association is reasonably linear or influenced by this boundary.
stages.decision: Calculate descriptive statistics and inspect the sleep–score scatterplot, identifying a possible upper score boundary before interpreting Pearson's r.
stages.rejected: A large correlation by itself would not establish that the relationship is linear over all sleep durations or transferable to another class.

notebook.dataSummary: 30 wholly synthetic student rows, no duplicate IDs. Sleep mean 6.98 hours (range 4.8–9.2); quiz mean 92.32 (range 75.2–100.0). Six quiz scores equal 100. Pearson r = .7472, p = 2.10 × 10⁻⁶, calculated from the invented values.

stages.forward: Choose an association estimate while making the observed range and ceiling pattern visible in the report.
compare: Does the scatterplot suggest linearity or a bounded-score pattern?
Could one summary conceal clinically or educationally important variation?

stages.title: Choose and justify the analysis
stages.where: The student chooses a numerical association estimate appropriate to the observational question.
stages.changed: Pearson correlation is justified by the two student-level numerical variables, while its interpretation is qualified by score limits and the constructed sample.
reasoning: The sample Pearson correlation compares two numerical measurements in paired student records, without treating reported sleep as experimentally assigned.
The independent student IDs avoid within-student repeated-measures dependence, but the class is still a convenience setting and does not support a population-random inference.
The score ceiling, potential nonlinearity, unrecorded confounders and the fictional nature of the data all matter when reporting uncertainty.
stages.decision: Use Pearson's r for this synthetic demonstration, report the effect as a sample association and examine the scatterplot rather than relying on significance alone.
stages.rejected: A p-value below .05 does not establish causation, a general population effect or the validity of an undocumented quiz instrument.

notebook.analysisChoice: Pearson correlation across 30 paired synthetic student records. Report r = .7472 and the corresponding two-sided test p ≈ 2.10 × 10⁻⁶ for an illustrative independent-pairs model; inspect the upper quiz-score boundary and avoid empirical generalisation.

stages.forward: The Results should distinguish a reproducible statistic from a claim about real students.
compare: Which assumptions depend on how students were sampled and measured?
What would the correlation mean if the entire dataset had been deliberately constructed?

stages.title: Write the Results or findings
stages.where: The Results text reports a transparent numerical pattern without adding causal explanations.
stages.changed: The single statistical sentence becomes a traceable report of the student count, observed ranges and synthetic correlation.
reasoning: The source CSV has 30 paired sleep and quiz measurements with one row per synthetic student.
The calculated Pearson correlation is .7472 and the associated model-based two-sided p-value is approximately 2.10 × 10⁻⁶.
A number of quiz values sit at the upper score boundary, so the positive pattern should be shown with a scatterplot as well as a coefficient.
stages.decision: State the descriptive values, the Pearson association and the synthetic status together, without implying that sleep produced the scores.
stages.rejected: Students with more sleep earned higher grades because sleep improved memory would overstate the evidence and invent a measured mechanism.

notebook.result1: Across 30 synthetic student rows, reported sleep averaged 6.98 hours (range 4.8–9.2) and quiz scores averaged 92.32 (range 75.2–100.0). The sample Pearson correlation was r = .7472, with a model-based two-sided p ≈ 2.10 × 10⁻⁶. Six records had the maximum score of 100.0.

stages.forward: The Discussion can now connect this fabricated pattern with the real literature without pretending its magnitude was observed.
compare: Could another student reproduce r from the supplied 30 records?
Does your Results section report only what was measured or computed?

stages.title: Write the Discussion and limitations
stages.where: The student distinguishes possible mechanisms from what an observational correlation can actually establish.
stages.changed: Interpretation now addresses confounding, uncertainty and the large difference between the synthetic result and published pooled findings.
reasoning: Dewald et al. (2010) estimated a much smaller pooled sleep-duration association with school performance, r = .069; the synthetic r = .7472 was constructed and cannot validate or contradict that research.
Sleep duration was not assigned, and different patterns of study, attendance, prior achievement or stress could contribute to associations in real records.
The quiz-score upper boundary, missing source instruments, single hypothetical class and lack of temporal information further limit what the example could mean as an empirical study.
stages.decision: Use the fabricated association to teach careful observational reporting, alongside a clear explanation of why it cannot support advice that increasing sleep would raise a student's quiz score.
stages.rejected: Describing the large synthetic coefficient as a replicated biological or educational effect would confuse an instructional calculation with genuine research.

notebook.limitations: The 30 rows are invented. A comparable real study would face self-report error, a convenience sample, potential confounding, unverified quiz scoring, the observed 100-point ceiling and no recorded temporal ordering. The fictitious p-value cannot establish a real population association.

stages.forward: The conclusion and abstract should remain understandable without access to the dataset and clearly distinguish the real literature from fictional results.
compare: How does your interpretation change when you know the observations were generated for instruction?
Which alternative explanations could only be examined with additional records or designs?

stages.title: Write the conclusion, abstract, title, and keywords
stages.where: The student prepares a descriptive conclusion and stand-alone abstract that preserve the synthetic and observational boundaries.
stages.changed: The closing text combines the true design, quantitative illustration and its limited meaning without claiming a classroom effect.
reasoning: Name the predictor, outcome and observational design in the title without using the language of causal intervention.
Report 30 synthetic records and Pearson r approximately .75, with the invented status evident in the abstract.
Close on what the example teaches about student-level association and the need for independent validation rather than a sleep recommendation.
stages.decision: Use an observational title and an abstract that labels every numerical finding as synthetic and identifies potential confounding.
stages.rejected: The effect of additional sleep on biology grades would describe a causal quantity the study cannot estimate.

notebook.title: Synthetic Observational Exemplar of Reported Weekday Sleep and Biology Quiz Scores
notebook.abstractDraft: This synthetic teaching exemplar illustrates an observational association between reported weekday sleep duration and biology quiz scores. The invented file includes 30 student-level records, each with a reported sleep value, weekly study-hours value and quiz score. Sleep averaged 6.98 hours, while quiz scores averaged 92.32. The Pearson association between reported sleep and score was r = .7472, with a model-based two-sided p ≈ 2.10 × 10⁻⁶. Six quiz values reached the observed maximum of 100, so score distribution and possible nonlinearity merit inspection. No sleep intervention, verified questionnaire, real student consent record or actual quiz administration is represented. Published reviews discuss sleep and learning, but they do not authenticate the constructed magnitude or establish its generality. The example demonstrates how to present a numerical association while recognising that confounding and measurement limitations prevent a causal interpretation.
notebook.keywords: reported sleep duration; biology quiz scores; observational research; Pearson correlation; synthetic data

stages.forward: The final audit should verify every reported number and every cited claim against the respective source.
compare: Does your abstract tell a reader immediately that the data are invented?
Would someone mistake your correlation for a policy recommendation if they read only the conclusion?

stages.title: Citations, references, and final alignment audit
stages.where: The final check traces both scholarly background and synthetic calculations to their sources.
stages.changed: A generic checklist becomes a specific audit of the research question, file columns, statistical output and claim limits.
reasoning: Verify the two article citations, including authors, publication details and DOIs, against scholarly bibliographic records.
Independently reconstruct the 30-row Pearson r and compare the result with the stored analysis output.
Confirm that the dataset, stage narrative and accompanying report call the records synthetic, name sleep as measured, and do not invent consent, a quiz rubric or causal intervention.
stages.decision: Retain the invented numerical example with a visible provenance statement and preserve the distinction between reproducible computation and empirical evidence.
stages.rejected: Calling an exact model-based p-value proof of a population relationship would remain wrong even if it were calculated without error.

notebook.audit: The two sleep review citations match PubMed and publisher records. The CSV contains 30 distinct student IDs, Pearson r = .7472007158832105 reproduces the statistical JSON, and the data are wholly synthetic. Study instruments, consent, actual recruitment and a causal identification strategy are not documented.

stages.forward: The research chain is now auditable at repository-source level; a real classroom inquiry would need its own authorised data, documented measures and evidence-bounded claims.
compare: Is the provenance of every statistic clearly stated?
What genuine records would a real study require that this teaching example does not contain?

projects.title: Retrieval Routine in Two Pre-Existing Classes
projects.subtitle: Quasi-experimental exemplar with baseline, selection, and causal-boundary reasoning
projects.rq: How did pre-to-post biology scores change in a class using a retrieval-practice routine compared with a pre-existing comparison class?
projects.disclaimer: The two cited retrieval-practice experiments are real scholarly publications. Both class groups, all 48 student records and every result in this exemplar are synthetic teaching material. Only one class represents each instructional condition, so no valid class-level treatment-effect test or causal estimate is available.
projects.data_summary: 48 synthetic student records across two pre-existing classes (24 each). After reconciling change scores with the displayed pre/post values, the class means change by 9.72 and 3.30 points, a descriptive difference of 6.43 points. One class per condition prevents valid class-level treatment-effect inference.

sources.citation: Roediger, H. L., III, & Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science, 17(3), 249–255. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2006.01693.x
sources.use: Experimental evidence that retrieval practice can improve delayed retention compared with restudying educationally relevant prose passages in the tested conditions.
sources.boundary: The 2006 experiments used controlled study conditions and delayed memory assessments. They do not describe or establish comparability between the two invented intact biology classes.

sources.citation: Karpicke, J. D., & Blunt, J. R. (2011). Retrieval practice produces more learning than elaborative studying with concept mapping. Science, 331(6018), 772–775. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1199327
sources.use: Experimental evidence that retrieval practice can support meaningful learning from science-related texts compared with elaborative concept mapping in the tested tasks.
sources.boundary: The study's controlled comparison, material and assessments are different from the fabricated pre/post biology-class dataset; it does not substantiate the invented class difference.

stages.title: Find a research interest
stages.where: A teacher wonders whether regular opportunities to retrieve biological concepts could be examined using the classes already on the timetable.
stages.changed: A general interest in retrieval practice becomes a question about a feasible comparison of existing classroom routines.
reasoning: Identify what counts as retrieval practice, such as recalling material without consulting notes before receiving feedback.
Consider whether pre- and post-assessments can address the same intended knowledge and reasoning without introducing a different score scale.
Recognise early that different intact classes may vary in ways unrelated to a teaching routine.
stages.decision: Explore a short retrieval-practice routine as an instructional change to describe within one existing class alongside another class's scores.
stages.rejected: Assuming that any difference between two classes shows the routine's effect would ignore differences that existed before the routine.

notebook.startingQuestion: How might scores change in an existing class using retrieval practice compared with a different class following its usual routine?

stages.forward: The available timetable and assessments now set the feasible sample and the limits of comparison.
compare: What could you reasonably observe within existing classroom routines?
Which classroom differences could already influence the result?

stages.title: Narrow the topic and test feasibility
stages.where: The student narrows the illustration to two pre-existing classes with 24 fictional records each.
stages.changed: The proposed study becomes a before-and-after comparison of scores in the same students, with each class attached to one routine.
reasoning: Two groups of 24 records allow practice linking pre- and post-scores within students.
An intact class receives the retrieval routine and the other serves as a comparison; no student-level or class-level random assignment occurs.
The source does not specify teaching duration, assessment rubric or implementation records, so those details must be presented as requirements for any real study.
stages.decision: Use a hypothetical two-class comparison with 48 student-level paired observations, and acknowledge that the teaching condition is inseparable from class identity.
stages.rejected: Calling the classes equivalent because each has 24 students would mistake equal sample size for comparability.

notebook.scope: One synthetic retrieval class and one synthetic comparison class, with pre- and post-scores for each of 24 students.
notebook.feasibility: A real project would require compatible assessments, documented instructional routines, a defined timeline, appropriate consent and data access. None is supplied by the fabricated file.

stages.forward: Scholarly background can establish why retrieval practice is relevant without validating this particular class contrast.
compare: What information would you need to know about the two classes before comparing their changes?
Which planned details cannot be inferred from a synthetic spreadsheet?

stages.title: Explore the research landscape
stages.where: The student reads experimental research on retrieval practice while keeping the school comparison's design distinct.
stages.changed: The research rationale now connects delayed retrieval outcomes and conceptual learning to the proposed biology task.
reasoning: Roediger and Karpicke (2006) compared retrieval testing and restudying in controlled studies using written passages and delayed retention tests.
Karpicke and Blunt (2011) compared retrieval practice with elaborative concept-mapping study and reported an advantage on learning assessments using science-related texts.
Those experiments support the relevance of retrieval as a learning activity, but they do not remove differences between two pre-existing classes.
stages.decision: Retain retrieval-practice research as a theoretical and instructional rationale, without borrowing the studies' causal conclusions for this invented comparison.
stages.rejected: The statement that retrieval practice necessarily caused a larger score change in the fictional class is not supported by the cited literature.

notebook.known: Controlled experimental studies have reported benefits of retrieval practice on delayed retention and conceptual learning in their tested conditions.
notebook.uncertain: The reasons for score changes in two actual intact classes would require local implementation, measurement and contextual evidence.

stages.forward: An answerable question should compare recorded changes without asserting an identifiable treatment effect.
compare: What do the published researchers compare that differs from these two intact classes?
Can experimental findings elsewhere justify a question without proving your classroom result?

stages.title: Write and refine the research question
stages.where: The research question is finalised as a comparison of pre-to-post scores rather than an estimated treatment effect.
stages.changed: The wording gives a clear outcome and time structure while limiting the inference to the two selected classes.
reasoning: Link pre- and post-scores within students and then describe each class's average change.
Specify the retrieval routine and the comparison class without implying randomised allocation.
Avoid promising a causal effect or a general population estimate when only one intact class represents each condition.
stages.decision: How did pre-to-post biology scores change in a class using a retrieval-practice routine compared with a pre-existing comparison class?
stages.rejected: How much did the retrieval routine increase learning? This would require a causal comparison the two-class example cannot identify.

notebook.finalRQ: How did pre-to-post biology scores change in a class using a retrieval-practice routine compared with a pre-existing comparison class?
notebook.rqJustification: The question concerns an instructional change, so its broad question family is Experimental. The specific design is quasi-experimental, and the single-class-per-condition illustration supports descriptive change only, not identification of an intervention effect.

stages.forward: The literature search and study plan now need to preserve the distinctions between retrieval studies and descriptive intact-class comparisons.
compare: Does the question still have a meaningful answer if causation cannot be established?
Could readers mistake a comparison of two classes for replicated treatment evidence?

stages.title: Build a systematic search strategy
stages.where: The student plans how to find retrieval-practice studies and appropriate quasi-experimental design guidance.
stages.changed: The search plan identifies the instructional activity, learning outcomes and method limitations rather than looking only for positive results.
reasoning: Use related terms such as retrieval practice, practice testing and test-enhanced learning for the intervention concept.
Pair them with retention, science learning or assessment outcomes to locate relevant empirical work.
Search separately for intact-class comparison, pretest-posttest design and classroom-level clustering to examine inferential limitations.
stages.decision: Document background searches by query, source system and date, without pretending the two available papers constitute an exhaustive review.
stages.rejected: Searching only for studies that prove retrieval improves grades would shape source selection around an assumed conclusion.

notebook.searchLogic: ('retrieval practice' OR 'practice testing' OR 'test-enhanced learning') AND (learning OR retention OR science); add a separate search for intact-class quasi-experimental comparison and clustering.
notebook.searchLogRule: Record actual databases, dates, strings, filters and screening decisions. No historic search log or source counts accompany this example.

stages.forward: Source extraction can then distinguish experimental retrieval evidence from methods advice about two existing classrooms.
compare: Which search terms could find null or conflicting retrieval-practice results?
How would you document a search without inventing records of searches never made?

stages.title: Evaluate, read, and extract sources
stages.where: The student appraises two genuine experimental articles as research background.
stages.changed: Rather than treating citations as endorsements of the fictional result, the account considers participants, outcome type and intervention structure.
reasoning: Roediger and Karpicke (2006) tested delayed retention following retrieval and restudy conditions with educationally relevant prose.
Karpicke and Blunt (2011) examined retrieval-based learning and concept mapping, including assessments of inference and comprehension.
Neither article documents the two fictional biology classes, their pre/post tests or their classroom routines.
stages.decision: Retain both citations with explicit boundaries and record that their experimental conclusions are not transferable without considering the local design.
stages.rejected: Using these published experiments to label two existing classes as experimentally exchangeable would misrepresent the studies.

notebook.sourceExtraction: Q-S01 concerns retrieval tests and delayed prose retention. Q-S02 compares retrieval practice with concept mapping for science-relevant textual learning. Their controlled contrasts differ from a one-class-per-condition before-and-after example.

stages.forward: A literature synthesis should explain why retrieval practice deserves study while recognising that the local example cannot support the same causal inference.
compare: What was actually assigned or compared in the published work?
Does a source's use of biology-related material match the exact quiz and conditions of this illustration?

stages.title: Synthesize the literature and justify the study
stages.where: The research rationale is developed without inventing a gap or an observed intervention benefit.
stages.changed: The exemplar becomes a methodological demonstration of linking score changes and interpreting classroom differences cautiously.
reasoning: Published retrieval studies provide background for why retrieval could be an educationally interesting routine.
An intact-class comparison can describe how scores changed during a particular classroom period.
Because the routine appears in only one class, a change difference is also a difference between the particular classes and cannot isolate the routine.
stages.decision: Frame the project as an instructional illustration of a quasi-experimental before-and-after comparison, with the selection and class-confounding problem central to the rationale.
stages.rejected: Claiming that the example replicates a randomised retrieval experiment would conceal major design differences.

notebook.rationale: Use two fictional intact classes to teach score linkage, descriptive change and the limits of attributing between-class differences to instructional practice.

stages.forward: The literature review can now connect prior experimental evidence with the more limited classroom comparison.
compare: Why can a comparison still be educationally useful when it does not identify a treatment effect?
How might a better study create replication at the class level?

stages.title: Write the literature review
stages.where: The student joins the two published findings into a discussion that leads to a bounded comparison question.
stages.changed: The literature account now follows an intellectual thread from retrieval and retention to the difficulty of translating controlled comparisons into intact classrooms.
reasoning: Retrieval testing may influence later retention, as studied by Roediger and Karpicke (2006), under specified assessment delays.
Karpicke and Blunt (2011) extend the rationale to conceptual learning with science-related texts and comparisons to elaborative study.
The proposed before-and-after class comparison would address a different outcome and leave class composition, teacher practice and other contextual factors uncontrolled.
stages.decision: Use a connected literature passage that explains the proposed routine and also prepares readers for why the class contrast has weaker inferential status.
stages.rejected: An article-by-article list that ends by predicting a numerical benefit would overstate how directly the published results apply.

notebook.literatureReviewPlan: Retrieving knowledge can be part of learning, and controlled experiments have examined its consequences for delayed retention and meaningful learning (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006; Karpicke & Blunt, 2011). A classroom comparison of pre-to-post biology scores asks a narrower local question. Unlike the published controlled experiments, the instructional example assigns one intact class to each routine, so any difference in change also reflects unseparated class-level conditions.

stages.forward: The Method must now identify which units are independently exposed to the routines and how scores will be linked across time.
compare: Does the literature discussion explain the transition from controlled tests to intact classrooms?
Have you kept the specific causal claims attached to the designs that produced them?

stages.title: Choose the research design
stages.where: The design is chosen after recognising that existing classes receive the instructional conditions.
stages.changed: The example is labelled quasi-experimental, but the class-level contrast is explicitly descriptive because each condition has one class.
reasoning: Twenty-four records are nested in each of two intact classes; the instructional routine varies only between classes.
There is no class replication within either instructional condition and no random assignment.
With one class per condition, a class-specific feature is inseparable from the routine, so a student-level test cannot yield a valid treatment-effect interval.
stages.decision: Use a two-group quasi-experimental teaching design for describing paired score changes, without claiming valid inference about the routine's causal effect.
stages.rejected: Calling 24 students per class independent treatment replications would mistake within-class observations for replicated instructional conditions.

notebook.title: Synthetic Quasi-Experimental Exemplar of Paired Biology Scores in Two Pre-Existing Classes
notebook.abstractDraft: This synthetic instructional example examines paired biology score records from two pre-existing classes, one labelled retrieval_routine and the other comparison_class. Each contains 24 invented student records. The mean pre- and post-scores are 69.18 and 78.90 in the retrieval class and 68.66 and 71.96 in the comparison class, yielding mean increases of 9.72 and 3.30 points. The descriptive difference between mean changes is 6.43 points. Because a single class represents each instructional condition, class characteristics cannot be separated from the routine. Student-level significance tests and confidence intervals would therefore be invalid for estimating a class-level treatment effect. The files are fictitious teaching material, and their calculations do not establish that retrieval practice improved students' scores.

projects.title: Multilingual Students Explaining Data-Rich Biology Questions

notebook.title: Synthetic Qualitative Exemplar of Multilingual Students' Accounts of Biology Explanations
notebook.abstractDraft: This teaching exemplar uses eight fictional statements attributed to imagined multilingual secondary students discussing data-rich biology questions in English. Each statement has a participant identifier and an initial code. A simplified thematic exercise groups four excerpts about wording and task interpretation, three describing visual, peer or Korean-language resources, and one account of sentence starters alongside the desire to choose evidence. The single-excerpt grouping is explicitly tentative. The material contains no complete transcripts, actual interview context, consent or classroom observations, and its themes are provisional interpretations of invented accounts rather than findings about learners. The exercise demonstrates how an analyst can preserve quotations, connect codes to excerpts and recognise the difference between a plausible interpretation and a defensible empirical claim.
