projects.title: Language and Participation in Secondary Science Inquiry
projects.subtitle: Mini literature-review exemplar with real source records and bounded coverage claims
projects.rq: What considerations for language and participation in secondary science investigation can be drawn from three selected education publications, and what limits their interpretation?
projects.disclaimer: Four genuine publications are supplied for teaching. Three are selected science/STEM education sources, and the fourth is the PRISMA 2020 reporting guideline. There is no documented database search, screening history or systematic review, and this small conceptual comparison does not establish field-wide findings.
projects.data_summary: Four authentic source records, including three selected education publications (LR-S01–LR-S03) and one reporting-guideline reference (LR-S04). The matrix illustrates limited conceptual synthesis, not a systematic search or a four-study empirical review.

notebook.limitations: Purposefully chosen three-text domain set with mixed genres; PRISMA is methods-only. No documented comprehensive search, eligibility criteria, flow counts, primary-study extractions, risk-of-bias assessment or protocol. A conceptual intersection cannot be treated as a field-wide empirical consensus.

stages.forward: The abstract should make the distinction between an instructional reading set and a conducted systematic or scoping review unmistakable.
compare: Which limitations affect the evidence base, and which affect the scope of the question itself?
What further studies would need to be examined before recommending a specific intervention?

stages.title: Write the conclusion, abstract, title, and keywords
stages.where: The title, abstract and conclusion are drafted after clarifying the exact source count and purpose.
stages.changed: The closing material describes an honest three-source education comparison with one reporting reference.
reasoning: Use a title that reflects selected sources and avoids systematic-review or meta-analysis terminology.
Identify the 2013 article and 2018 and 2019 consensus reports as domain sources, while PRISMA supplies a separate reporting principle.
Report that the exercise develops considerations rather than estimates treatment effects or establishes comprehensive thematic recurrence.
stages.decision: Use a self-contained abstract and title explicitly identifying a purposive conceptual mini-review.
stages.rejected: Calling four publications a systematic review with confirmed recurring findings would imply a review design absent from the records.

notebook.title: Selected-Source Mini-Review Exemplar of Language and Participation in Secondary Science
notebook.abstractDraft: This instructional mini-review considers what three selected education publications contribute to understanding language and participation in secondary science investigation. One conceptual article discusses language within science practices, a 2018 consensus report examines English learners' resources and access in STEM, and a 2019 consensus report centres investigation and design in Grades 6–12. A fourth publication, the PRISMA 2020 reporting guideline, is used only to explain what a systematically conducted review would need to document. Read together, the three education texts invite consideration of how disciplinary language and equitable participation relate to opportunities for reasoning with evidence. Their differing scopes, populations and publication genres limit this comparison. No database search log, screening history, effect estimates or comprehensive review protocol are supplied, so the observations are an illustrative conceptual synthesis rather than field-wide findings.
notebook.keywords: multilingual science education; English learners; disciplinary language; science investigation; conceptual literature review

stages.forward: A final audit must verify the source identities, row count, attribution and absence of invented search or effect claims.
compare: Could a reader mistake this teaching exercise for a systematic or scoping review?
Does the abstract explain the purpose of the methods guideline separately?

stages.title: Citations, references, and final alignment audit
stages.where: The student verifies the source-to-synthesis links and the review's declared limits.
stages.changed: The final checks name the four publication types, three-source synthesis and missing review-process records.
reasoning: Check all four publication titles, authorship, dates and DOIs against publishers or authoritative institutional sites.
Confirm one matrix row per reference ID, with three domain records and one methods-only PRISMA record.
Ensure no search counts, screened-record totals, quotations, primary-study effect sizes, registered protocol or field-wide claims are invented in the stages or paper.
stages.decision: Preserve the three-publication conceptual comparison, maintain PRISMA's reporting-only status and disclose the incomplete evidence-selection trail.
stages.rejected: Attaching a fabricated PRISMA flowchart or declaring systematic search coverage would undermine scholarly integrity.

notebook.audit: Four authoritative bibliographic records were checked. LR-S01–LR-S03 are selected education texts; LR-S04 is PRISMA 2020 methods guidance. The repository lacks a dated search, screening and appraisal history, and no empirical outcome synthesis can be verified from the selected matrix.

stages.forward: The source-level teaching exemplar is complete following final data/source parity checks; a systematic review would require its own recorded search and study-selection procedures.
compare: Does every sentence in the synthesis stay within a cited source's remit?
Which research records would be needed before promoting this exercise into a systematic review?

projects.title: Synthetic Meta-Analysis of a Learning Intervention
projects.subtitle: Meta-analysis mechanics exemplar with effect units, heterogeneity, and model reasoning
projects.rq: What pooled standardised mean difference results from applying a DerSimonian–Laird random-effects calculation to eight hypothetical effect estimates?
projects.disclaimer: All eight effect estimates, their standard errors and the resulting pooled calculations are synthetic. The three cited papers are genuine methodology sources; no primary intervention reports, original outcome data, selection log, evidence of independence or real systematic review are supplied.
projects.data_summary: Eight invented g/SE pairs (T01–T08). DerSimonian–Laird random-effects pooled g = 0.3688, normal-approximation 95% CI [0.2632, 0.4743], Q(7) = 8.0729, τ² = 0.00309, I² = 13.29%. These are reproducible teaching calculations, not empirical treatment evidence.

sources.citation: Borenstein, M., Hedges, L. V., Higgins, J. P. T., & Rothstein, H. R. (2010). A basic introduction to fixed-effect and random-effects models for meta-analysis. Research Synthesis Methods, 1(2), 97–111. https://doi.org/10.1002/jrsm.12
sources.use: Explains how fixed-effect and random-effects pooling embody different assumptions about underlying effects, providing background for the DerSimonian–Laird illustration.
sources.boundary: The publication supplies statistical methodology, not T01–T08, and does not validate the independence or source data of the fictional effect estimates.

sources.citation: Higgins, J. P. T., Thompson, S. G., Deeks, J. J., & Altman, D. G. (2003). Measuring inconsistency in meta-analyses. BMJ, 327(7414), 557–560. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.327.7414.557
sources.use: Presents and interprets the I² inconsistency measure used alongside Cochran's Q in meta-analysis.
sources.boundary: I² is a descriptive measure, sensitive to the available study set, and does not identify causes of heterogeneity or certify a homogeneous intervention effect.

sources.citation: Page, M. J., McKenzie, J. E., Bossuyt, P. M., Boutron, I., Hoffmann, T. C., Mulrow, C. D., Shamseer, L., Tetzlaff, J. M., Akl, E. A., Brennan, S. E., Chou, R., Glanville, J., Grimshaw, J. M., Hróbjartsson, A., Lalu, M. M., Li, T., Loder, E. W., Mayo-Wilson, E., McDonald, S., ... Moher, D. (2021). The PRISMA 2020 statement: An updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews. BMJ, 372, n71. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.n71
sources.use: Guidance for transparent reporting of actual systematic-review searches, screening, appraisal and synthesis procedures.
sources.boundary: No primary studies or search, selection and appraisal records exist for the fictional effect set, so citing PRISMA does not make the worked calculation a conducted systematic review.

stages.title: Find a research interest
stages.where: A student wonders how quantitative findings from more than one intervention study could be considered together.
stages.changed: The interest moves from the effectiveness of a learning intervention to the calculations and assumptions involved in pooling comparable results.
reasoning: Different studies may estimate similar educational outcomes on scales that are not directly comparable.
A standardised mean difference can express a contrast relative to its variability, provided the measures and comparisons warrant synthesis.
Constructed effect estimates offer a way to practise the calculation without claiming to have identified research about a real intervention.
stages.decision: Explore what a meta-analysis does when estimates are placed on a shared scale and assigned weights reflecting their uncertainty.
stages.rejected: A claim that a particular learning intervention works cannot be supported by invented effects.

notebook.startingQuestion: How can several comparable effect estimates be combined, and how do their uncertainties influence the answer?

stages.forward: The next stage should define the hypothetical studies and what the existing extraction file can actually substantiate.
compare: What conditions would make different intervention outcomes suitable for a common effect metric?
Are you investigating an intervention or demonstrating a statistical method?

stages.title: Narrow the topic and test feasibility
stages.where: The exercise is bounded to eight invented effect-estimate rows instead of a real evidence base.
stages.changed: Its scope is defined by the exact study identifiers, effect values and standard errors supplied in a synthetic CSV.
reasoning: Each of T01–T08 has a value labelled standardised_mean_difference_g and a corresponding standard_error.
The source does not contain the sample sizes, outcome distributions or primary reports needed to recompute each individual g.
Study independence and measurement comparability are assumptions of the illustration, not facts verified through real reports.
stages.decision: Use the eight fictional effects to demonstrate a specific random-effects pooling algorithm with a clearly limited inferential interpretation.
stages.rejected: Describing the eight effects as eight independently verified experiments would invent study designs and participant information.

notebook.scope: Eight invented effect estimates and eight positive standard errors, one row for each T01–T08.
notebook.feasibility: The extracted inputs are sufficient to reproduce one simplified inverse-variance meta-analysis. They are insufficient to verify effect-size generation, actual study independence, search coverage or study quality.

stages.forward: Methodology sources can now establish the distinctions among pooling models, heterogeneity and reporting.
compare: Which calculations can you verify from the available columns?
Which features of a real meta-analysis would require primary-study records?

stages.title: Explore the research landscape
stages.where: Three genuine methodology papers provide a basis for analysing the invented effect table.
stages.changed: Each source is assigned its specific function instead of being treated as intervention-effect evidence.
reasoning: Borenstein et al. (2010) explain how fixed-effect and random-effects models involve different assumptions and aims.
Higgins et al. (2003) introduce and discuss I² as a measure associated with between-study inconsistency, without identifying why estimates differ.
Page et al. (2021) provide the PRISMA 2020 reporting framework for real systematic reviews; its presence does not establish that this synthetic set was systematically selected.
stages.decision: Use the three publications for methodology only and keep the hypothetical effect sizes separate from their published evidence.
stages.rejected: Calling the methodological citations eight real learning-intervention studies would confuse guidance with observations.

notebook.known: The selected publications explain model assumptions, heterogeneity interpretation and transparent review reporting.
notebook.uncertain: The eight effect sizes were invented, so there is no verified source of their intervention outcomes, independent sampling or risk of bias.

stages.forward: The research question can focus on a reproducible synthetic calculation rather than a claim about an intervention's effectiveness.
compare: Which methodological claims can a citation support without supplying any intervention effects?
How might the interpretation change under a different pooling model?

stages.title: Write and refine the research question
stages.where: The question names the specific statistical procedure and acknowledges the hypothetical character of the input.
stages.changed: An open question about a real intervention's pooled effect becomes a reproducible teaching question.
reasoning: The effects have been labelled g, but the original group statistics needed to check Hedges' correction are not available.
DerSimonian–Laird random-effects pooling can be reconstructed from g and its standard error for each row.
The question should ask what that calculation produces, without presupposing the existence of eight independently recruited studies.
stages.decision: What pooled standardised mean difference results from applying a DerSimonian–Laird random-effects calculation to eight hypothetical effect estimates?
stages.rejected: What is the proven effect of the learning intervention? This would turn fabricated study-level estimates into a real educational conclusion.

notebook.finalRQ: What pooled standardised mean difference results from applying a DerSimonian–Laird random-effects calculation to eight hypothetical effect estimates?
notebook.rqJustification: Eight synthetic g/SE pairs support reconstruction of one specified random-effects calculation. They do not document real interventions, study selection or underlying participant measures.

stages.forward: The next stages should explain how a genuine systematic search and an auditable effect extraction would be conducted.
compare: Can someone answer the question directly from the stored CSV?
Does the question promise an empirical claim that a synthetic table cannot deliver?

stages.title: Build a systematic search strategy
stages.where: The student considers how real review searches would produce study-level inputs before pooling.
stages.changed: A hypothetical search procedure is separated from the undocumented origin of the teaching data.
reasoning: A real intervention review would specify population, intervention, comparator, outcomes and eligible study designs.
Search strings, database names, dates, de-duplication and screening decisions would be archived before reporting a flow of studies.
No such search or selection history accompanies these eight invented rows.
stages.decision: Illustrate a prospective systematic search plan while explicitly recording that no search yielded T01–T08.
stages.rejected: A fabricated PRISMA flow in which eight studies were retrieved and included would imply research activity that never happened.

notebook.searchLogic: For a future real review, combine intervention terms with relevant learner, comparison and outcome concepts; specify actual databases and adapt their search syntax.
notebook.searchLogRule: Preserve exact search queries and dates, all retrieved identifiers, duplicate and exclusion decisions, and full-text sources. None exists for the invented effects.

stages.forward: Source appraisal must next distinguish methodology articles from the absent primary intervention studies.
compare: Which review records would substantiate that eight empirical studies were selected?
Why can PRISMA guidance not stand in for having performed those steps?

stages.title: Evaluate, read, and extract sources
stages.where: The three literature records are evaluated for the methodological contributions they actually make.
stages.changed: A method paper is not treated as a source of fictional effect estimates or a verification of primary-study quality.
reasoning: Borenstein et al. describe model assumptions, supporting explicit selection of a random-effects calculation.
Higgins et al. examine inconsistency measures, highlighting that an I² value alone cannot explain heterogeneity.
PRISMA 2020 concerns the reporting of real searches, selection and analysis, none of which can be retrospectively assumed for fictional T01–T08.
stages.decision: Record each citation's methodological role and boundary, noting that no underlying intervention papers were available to appraise.
stages.rejected: A verified DOI does not make an artificial effect estimate an independently verified study result.

notebook.sourceExtraction: M-S01 informs random-effects model assumptions; M-S02 informs Q/I² interpretation; M-S03 informs transparent review reporting. The three sources are methodology references, not the primary reports for T01–T08.

stages.forward: The rationale can focus on learning the quantitative method without manufacturing a claim of research novelty.
compare: Which source defines the calculation, and which addresses reporting?
Would a real review require additional information beyond the abstract of each intervention report?

stages.title: Synthesize the literature and justify the study
stages.where: The rationale moves from a teaching need to the actual limitations of pooled statistics.
stages.changed: The project is justified as a transparent computational demonstration rather than a synthesis of an intervention literature.
reasoning: Combining effects requires decisions about a common metric and the distribution of plausible underlying effects.
Random-effects weighting includes an estimated between-study variance, so results depend on modelling assumptions as well as input standard errors.
A small invented dataset can make these steps visible while teaching why plausible-looking confidence intervals must not be mistaken for empirical evidence.
stages.decision: Use the fictional table to show how an estimate is calculated and why model choice and uncertainty need careful explanation.
stages.rejected: Stating that no meta-analysis of this intervention exists would require a genuine search and an identified intervention.

notebook.rationale: The synthetic example is a worked illustration of inverse-variance random-effects pooling, heterogeneity and reporting limits using traceable numeric inputs.

stages.forward: The background section should connect model choice to heterogeneity and appropriate reporting without a mechanical list of references.
compare: What does the random-effects framework assume about study estimates?
How can an instructional numerical result seem credible even when its underlying studies do not exist?

stages.title: Write the literature review
stages.where: The literature section develops how the choice of pooling model changes what is estimated.
stages.changed: The narrative connects model assumptions, inconsistency and transparent reporting through their methodological implications.
reasoning: A fixed-effect analysis assumes one underlying effect, while a random-effects analysis models variation in underlying effects among studies.
A measure such as I² helps describe inconsistency, although it does not determine which research settings explain differences.
Real reviews must report how their studies were found and assessed; because the present inputs are invented, those reporting steps cannot be filled with fictional details.
stages.decision: Build a methods rationale that leads from effect-size comparability through modelling to transparent presentation of uncertainty.
stages.rejected: Treating a small I² as proof that all eight fictional interventions are identical would misinterpret the statistic.

notebook.literatureReviewPlan: Borenstein et al. (2010) distinguish the assumptions and purposes of fixed-effect and random-effects synthesis. Higgins et al. (2003) describe how inconsistency can be summarised, while warning against using heterogeneity measures as explanations. Page et al. (2021) provide reporting guidance that a genuine review would need to follow. These publications justify methodological care, not any empirical learning benefit.

stages.forward: The project can now state exactly which modelling procedure its source file allows.
compare: Can readers see how the statistical models differ before they see the numbers?
Which part of PRISMA reporting would remain impossible without original study records?

stages.title: Choose the research design
stages.where: The method is defined as a worked random-effects computation using eight invented g/SE pairs.
stages.changed: The design distinguishes a meta-analysis teaching calculation from a conducted systematic review with real independent studies.
reasoning: The source file contains eight effect estimates with positive standard errors, enabling inverse-variance weighting.
DerSimonian–Laird provides a moment estimate of the between-study variance τ² and an approximate pooled estimate.
Neither the underlying studies' independence nor their outcome comparability can be confirmed from the file.
stages.decision: Use a DerSimonian–Laird random-effects instructional calculation with a conventional normal-approximation interval.
stages.rejected: Calling the worked calculation a systematic review demonstrating intervention efficacy would claim nonexistent empirical procedures.

notebook.claimBoundary: Reconstruct numerical pooling of eight synthetic input effects only. Normal-approximation uncertainty is conditional on simplifying assumptions and cannot be treated as real evidence about learning.

stages.forward: Define the units and exact variable names before computing any pooled quantities.
compare: What do the file's inputs permit you to compute directly?
What would you need to verify before asserting that effects are statistically independent?

stages.title: Define constructs, variables, or evidence units
stages.where: The student defines the synthetic effect as the unit of quantitative synthesis.
stages.changed: The data dictionary distinguishes each study ID, its stored g value and the uncertainty supplied as a standard error.
reasoning: The CSV has the exact fields study_id, standardized_mean_difference_g and standard_error, with T01–T08 unique.
A value labelled g implies a small-sample corrected standardised mean difference, but no raw group statistics are provided to verify its computation.
The estimates are treated as independent for this particular model illustration; no actual participant overlap, multiple outcomes or study design can be checked.
stages.decision: Treat each g/SE pair as an assumed independent synthetic effect and avoid claiming to have verified primary-study origins.
stages.rejected: Treating the eight effects as Hedges' g values calculated from confirmed experimental samples would invent underlying records.

notebook.effectMetric: Precomputed synthetic Hedges-type standardised mean difference labelled g; original means, standard deviations and sample sizes are absent.
notebook.unit: One putatively independent hypothetical effect estimate per T01–T08; the study identifier is a teaching label, not evidence of a real study.
notebook.uncertainty: Each row has a positive synthetic standard_error whose square is the within-effect variance for weighting.

stages.forward: A full review would establish compatible contrasts and address dependence before applying this extraction structure.
compare: Can the individual g estimates be reconstructed from their source data?
Could two reported effects share participants even when they have different identifiers?

stages.title: Plan sampling, measurement, validity, and ethics
stages.where: The analysis plan confronts the missing empirical details that would normally determine effect eligibility.
stages.changed: The sample description separates eight fabricated effects from eligibility rules and risk-of-bias procedures for actual studies.
reasoning: There are no real study populations, treatment assignments, participant counts or assessment instruments in the file.
A genuine review would specify comparable intervention, comparator, outcome and follow-up definitions before extracting any effect.
Study overlap, selective outcomes and risk of bias require primary reports; methodological citations cannot establish these characteristics for synthetic T01–T08.
stages.decision: Use all eight invented g/SE pairs as supplied for computation, without asserting a screened or independent empirical study sample.
stages.rejected: Describing positive effect estimates as eight successfully replicated benefits would overstate what fictional inputs can demonstrate.

notebook.sample: Eight invented rows, T01–T08, each with one effect estimate and one standard error. No primary-study sample sizes or consent/ethics records exist.
notebook.quality: A real review would check effect direction, comparators, study overlap, outcome definitions, study-level bias and reporting practices before synthesis.

stages.forward: The method should preserve the original input file and specify the estimator and its limitations.
compare: What information is required to judge whether studies should be pooled?
Would restricting a review to reported significant effects distort the synthesis?

stages.title: Write the method and lock the data plan
stages.where: The mathematical method is written as a reproducible sequence based on the original eight-row CSV.
stages.changed: The weighting and DerSimonian–Laird variance estimate are specified rather than reduced to a generic 'random effects' label.
reasoning: Calculate each variance vᵢ = SEᵢ² and fixed-effect weight 1/vᵢ to form the weighted preliminary mean and Cochran's Q.
Estimate τ² = max(0, (Q − (k − 1))/C), where C is the sum of fixed weights minus the squared-weight sum divided by the total weight.
Use random-effects weights 1/(vᵢ + τ²), calculate the weighted mean and its conventional standard error, then give an approximate normal 95% interval.
stages.decision: Reconstruct the exact DerSimonian–Laird moment estimator and conditional normal-approximation confidence interval from the eight supplied numbers.
stages.rejected: An arithmetic mean of the eight g values would ignore the differing standard errors and would not reproduce the specified model.

notebook.rowUnit: One T01–T08 synthetic effect with fields study_id, standardized_mean_difference_g, standard_error.
notebook.columns: study_id; standardized_mean_difference_g; standard_error. Compute within-effect variance from the squared standard error.
notebook.analysisIntent: Inverse-variance fixed-effect reference for Q; moment estimate of τ²; random-effects inverse-variance pooled g; normal-approximation interval; I² = max(0, (Q − df)/Q) × 100%.

stages.forward: Check for missing or duplicated rows, invalid standard errors, effect-scale inconsistencies and the sign convention before calculating results.
compare: Why does the algorithm first calculate fixed-effect weights even when reporting a random-effects pooled value?
Which assumptions are left out of the simple confidence interval?

stages.title: Collect or organise evidence
stages.where: The synthetic extraction is inspected before pooling all eight numeric effects.
stages.changed: The source checks are tied to the real CSV fields, value ranges and assumed direction of an effect.
reasoning: There are eight unique study identifiers and eight strictly positive standard errors, ranging from 0.11 to 0.19.
The stored g values range from 0.17 to 0.64 and all have the same positive sign, as constructed for this illustration.
No comparator descriptions or original effect calculations are available, so comparable direction and independence are modelling assumptions rather than verified study properties.
stages.decision: Retain all eight rows, preserve the exact supplied effect sizes and standard errors, and clearly identify the unverified interpretation of their positive signs.
stages.rejected: Treating positive signs as independent evidence that learners benefited would mistake fabricated numbers for real outcomes.

notebook.dataSummary: Eight synthetic g estimates, 0.17–0.64, and positive standard errors, 0.11–0.19. Every ID is distinct. The extracted effect values are sufficient to reproduce the stated DL calculation, without validating the original g computation.

stages.forward: The model can now be applied with explicit assumptions about between-effect variation and normal-approximation uncertainty.
compare: Do unique study labels establish independent samples?
What is the exact sign convention of the hypothetical intervention contrast?

stages.title: Choose and justify the analysis
stages.where: The student selects and executes an explicit inverse-variance random-effects calculation.
stages.changed: A generic request for heterogeneity statistics becomes a traceable model calculation with known assumptions.
reasoning: The fixed-effect reference mean is approximately 0.3656 and Cochran's Q is approximately 8.0729 with seven degrees of freedom.
DerSimonian–Laird estimates τ² = 0.003087, resulting in random-effects weights 1/(SE² + τ²).

The pooled estimate is approximately 0.36876 with a conventional normal-approximation standard error of 0.05386; this interval does not fully account for uncertainty in estimating τ² from eight inputs.
stages.decision: Report the DL pooled estimate and conditional normal interval while describing τ², Q and I² as properties of the synthetic calculation.
stages.rejected: Choosing the random-effects model after finding a low I², then declaring heterogeneity negligible, would misstate both model choice and statistic interpretation.

notebook.analysisChoice: DerSimonian–Laird random-effects model with τ² estimated by the method of moments, inverse-variance weights 1/(SEᵢ²+τ²), and approximate 95% interval g ± 1.96×SE. The small-k normal interval is illustrative, not a validated real-study precision claim.

stages.forward: The Results must report inputs and outputs without translating a fabricated g into real educational improvement.
compare: Could another estimator give a different heterogeneity estimate?
What does the normal approximation leave out when k is small?

stages.title: Write the Results or findings
stages.where: The Results give the exact numerical summary and the limits of its significance for real research.
stages.changed: The headline result is linked to the original input table and described as a synthetic model output.
reasoning: The eight g values produce random-effects pooled g = 0.3687617, with a normal-approximation 95% interval from approximately 0.2632 to 0.4743.
Cochran's Q = 8.0729 on seven degrees of freedom, the DL τ² estimate is 0.003087 and I² is approximately 13.29%.
These numbers are internally reproducible but cannot estimate the effectiveness of any observed learning intervention because the primary studies do not exist.
stages.decision: Present the pooled g, conditional interval, between-effect variance and inconsistency statistic with a prominent synthetic-data statement.
stages.rejected: An apparently positive 95% interval is not evidence that an actual teaching intervention works.

notebook.result1: From eight fictitious g/SE pairs, the DerSimonian–Laird pooled g is 0.3688, with normal-approximation 95% CI [0.2632, 0.4743]. Q(7) = 8.0729, τ² = 0.00309 and I² = 13.29%. Every result is synthetic.

stages.forward: The discussion should consider model and selection limits rather than recommending a classroom intervention.
compare: Can every value be recalculated from the supplied CSV?
Would a reader understand that the reported confidence interval has no real-study evidential status?

stages.title: Write the Discussion and limitations
stages.where: The statistical summary is considered alongside the uncertainty in its assumptions and origins.
stages.changed: The discussion explains the distinction between model-generated precision, heterogeneity and an empirically justified effect estimate.
reasoning: With eight hypothetical effects, the DL moment estimator and the normal confidence interval may behave differently from alternative estimators or small-sample methods.
I² describes a proportion of the observed dispersion statistic attributed to heterogeneity under a model; its small value does not prove identical effects or explain the variation.
The file provides neither searched-and-screened studies nor means, variances and sample sizes, so publication bias, study quality and dependence cannot be assessed.
stages.decision: Use the calculated values to teach model sensitivity and transparent interpretation, without any general statement about students or interventions.
stages.rejected: Calling I² = 13.29% proof of consistent educational benefits would mistake a descriptive heterogeneity measure for causal and evidential validation.

notebook.limitations: All g/SE pairs are invented; no empirical study designs, raw effect data, independence audit, risk-of-bias assessment, search process or publication-bias evidence exists. k = 8 is small, and the conventional DL normal interval does not incorporate all τ² uncertainty.

stages.forward: Closing material must identify the exercise as a model demonstration, including within its abstract.
compare: Could the apparent precision result from an unrealistic data-generation choice?
Does a low I² tell readers why study effects might differ?

stages.title: Write the conclusion, abstract, title, and keywords
stages.where: The conclusion and abstract are drafted to make statistical meaning understandable without overstating evidence.
stages.changed: The example identifies a specific method and every synthetic result while excluding claims about actual students.
reasoning: The title refers to eight invented effects and a worked random-effects calculation.
The abstract names the supplied g and standard-error inputs, pooled output and approximate interval.
The conclusion explains why mathematically reproducible model outputs cannot substitute for verified primary studies or review selection.
stages.decision: Write an abstract that gives the arithmetic and limitations in proportion to one another.
stages.rejected: Eight studies prove a learning intervention is effective would invent empirical research and misrepresent inference.

notebook.title: Synthetic Meta-Analysis Exemplar of Eight Hypothetical Intervention Effects
notebook.abstractDraft: This teaching exemplar reconstructs DerSimonian–Laird random-effects pooling from eight fictitious standardised mean differences and their standard errors. The synthetic values yield pooled g = 0.3688, with a conventional normal-approximation 95% interval from 0.2632 to 0.4743. The heterogeneity calculations give Q(7) = 8.0729, τ² = 0.00309 and I² = 13.29%. The underlying primary-study data, independence, study selection and risk of bias cannot be assessed because no real intervention reports are supplied. The interval illustrates one modelling procedure and is not an empirical estimate of learning-intervention effectiveness.
notebook.keywords: meta-analysis; DerSimonian–Laird; standardised mean difference; heterogeneity; synthetic evidence

stages.forward: The final audit compares every derived statistic and all three references against source documents.
compare: Does the abstract disclose that the primary studies are fictional before discussing outcomes?
Could the title be confused with an actual evidence synthesis?

stages.title: Citations, references, and final alignment audit
stages.where: The final audit links every data value and model output to reproducible calculations and genuine methodology sources.
stages.changed: Statistical verification is distinguished from what cannot be checked about hypothetical study provenance.
reasoning: The eight effect rows and the JSON model summary reproduce Q, τ², the pooled estimate and I², with no added or omitted input effect.
Borenstein et al. (2010) support distinguishing pooling models, Higgins et al. (2003) address I², and Page et al. (2021) concern reporting guidance.
No primary interventions, historical systematic search, overlapping-sample audit or individual-effect source data exist in the project, and the final paper must say so.
stages.decision: Retain the arithmetically verified synthetic results and explicitly record every inferential or empirical uncertainty.
stages.rejected: Representing methodological references as the sources of the fictional effect estimates would manufacture evidence.

notebook.audit: Eight unique T01–T08 g/SE pairs; DL Q ≈ 8.072862, τ² ≈ 0.00308714, pooled g ≈ 0.36876172 and I² ≈ 13.2897%; normal-approximation 95% interval ≈ [0.2632, 0.4743]. All values are teaching calculations with no real primary-study evidence.

stages.forward: Repository-level exemplar verification can close this stage; live application publication parity remains a separate task.
compare: Do the summary values match the formulas applied to the actual CSV?
Is every citation limited to claims it can genuinely support?

projects.title: Retrieval Practice, Score Change, and Student Experience
projects.subtitle: Mixed-methods exemplar showing separate strands and explicit integration
projects.rq: How did biology scores change during a retrieval-practice routine, how did students describe the routine, and how do the quantitative and qualitative findings jointly inform interpretation?
projects.disclaimer: The three background publications are genuine. The paired scores, six interview excerpts, initial codes, and mixed-methods interpretation are fictional teaching material, not conducted research.
projects.data_summary: Twenty-four synthetic score pairs yield a mean post-minus-pre change of 8.6958 points (paired-t 95% CI [6.1692, 11.2225]); 23 increase and one declines. Six fictional interviews are linked to positive-change cases only. The one-group design cannot establish causation.

stages.title: Find a research interest
stages.where: The example begins with two kinds of constructed classroom evidence, paired biology scores and brief student accounts of retrieval practice.
stages.changed: A general interest in how students study becomes a question about what score records and accounts of studying can each reveal.
reasoning: Paired scores can describe change within the same fictional students, while interview excerpts provide access to how six of them describe the routine.
Neither kind of record identifies why scores changed on its own. A mixed-methods question should preserve that distinction from the beginning.
The available files are instructional materials, not records of a study carried out with students.
stages.decision: Explore the relationship between the score pattern and student descriptions of retrieval, feedback, repetition and applying knowledge.
stages.rejected: A claim that retrieval practice caused improvements would exceed this one-group synthetic example.

notebook.broadTopic: Paired biology scores and student accounts of retrieval practice
notebook.startingQuestion: What do changes across 24 paired scores show, and how might six linked interview excerpts complicate their interpretation?

stages.forward: Stage 2 sets a scope that the constructed score table and six excerpts can genuinely support.
compare: Does your own project have two distinct forms of evidence, and what can each show?
Which limitations should shape your question before analysis begins?

stages.title: Narrow the topic and test feasibility
stages.where: The data files contain 24 student identifiers with paired scores and six excerpts linked to six of those identifiers.
stages.changed: The scope is restricted to a single fictional classroom scenario, two score observations per record and a small set of interview excerpts.
reasoning: There is no supplied timeline for the retrieval routine, assessment blueprint, score scale or interview sampling procedure.
A bounded demonstration can still teach paired analysis and evidence integration without supplying an invented school, participant history or intervention schedule.
The six excerpts should not be taken as a representative account of all 24 students.
stages.decision: Analyse the 24 constructed score pairs and examine the six available excerpts, joining records only through their shared identifiers.
stages.rejected: Long-term retention, transfer performance and a treatment effect cannot be established from these files.

notebook.scope: 24 fictional paired score records and six linked fictional interview excerpts
notebook.feasibility: Both files are available for source-level calculations and a six-case joint display; broader protocol details are unavailable.

stages.forward: Stage 3 identifies the research that motivates the teaching question without treating that literature as evidence from this fictional class.
compare: Where does your evidence set begin and end?
What information is absent, even though it might be useful in an actual study?

stages.title: Explore the research landscape
stages.where: Three authenticated publications provide learning-science and mixed-methods background, rather than participant data.
stages.changed: The literature has a separate role from the fictional classroom findings.
reasoning: Roediger and Karpicke (2006) tested retrieval and restudy under experimental conditions, including delayed retention tests.
Karpicke and Blunt (2011) compared retrieval practice with elaborative studying using concept maps.
Johnson and Onwuegbuzie (2004) discuss combining methods and reasoning across kinds of evidence. None reports these 24 scores or six interviews.
stages.decision: Use the first two papers to explain why retrieval merits investigation and the third to justify explicitly integrating the two types of evidence.
stages.rejected: Published retrieval effects cannot be assigned to this example's unverified routine or interpreted as its causal explanation.

notebook.known: Experimental research supports the general relevance of retrieval practice. Mixed-methods scholarship provides a rationale for coordinating different evidence forms.
notebook.uncertain: Whether this fictional score change reflects retrieval, test differences, maturation or other influences cannot be determined.

stages.forward: The question will distinguish a descriptive score comparison from accounts of experience and their eventual integration.
compare: Does each source directly support the purpose for which you cite it?
Which source claims would become misleading if moved into your own results section?

stages.title: Write and refine the research question
stages.where: The question is formulated to keep numerical change, reported experience and joint interpretation analytically distinct.
stages.changed: The final question includes a specific quantitative component, a qualitative component and a mixed-methods integration task.
reasoning: A paired score difference answers how the constructed scores changed, not what caused that difference.
The six snippets show particular reported experiences, without establishing how commonly those experiences occurred.
The integration asks what the linked records clarify or leave unresolved.
stages.decision: How did biology scores change during a retrieval-practice routine, how did students describe the routine, and how do the quantitative and qualitative findings jointly inform interpretation?
stages.rejected: Did retrieval practice improve biology learning? would imply a causal contrast that the scenario cannot support.

notebook.finalRQ: How did biology scores change during a retrieval-practice routine, how did students describe the routine, and how do the quantitative and qualitative findings jointly inform interpretation?
notebook.rqJustification: The question separates observed differences, reported accounts and interpretive integration; it makes no causal claim.

stages.forward: Stage 5 plans how to find and document relevant background sources without inventing a completed search.
compare: Can each part of your research question be answered with an identifiable evidence source?
Does any verb imply a causal inference the design cannot sustain?

stages.title: Build a systematic search strategy
stages.where: The three citations are available, but no original database search log is supplied.
stages.changed: A reproducible search plan is distinguished from an actually conducted literature search.
reasoning: A potential search could combine terms such as retrieval practice, testing effect, biology education, student experience and mixed methods.
Database names, exact queries, filters, dates and hit counts would need to be retained if a search were performed.
The presence of three verified papers does not demonstrate systematic coverage of a research field.
stages.decision: Draft two background search routes, one on retrieval and retention, another on classroom experience and mixed-methods integration, and label both as proposed.
stages.rejected: Do not invent databases searched, numbers retrieved or a comprehensive evidence gap.

notebook.searchLogic: Proposed route 1: ("retrieval practice" OR "testing effect") AND (learning OR biology). Proposed route 2: ("retrieval practice" OR "low-stakes quiz") AND (interview OR experience OR "mixed methods").
notebook.searchLogRule: If implemented, record source, search date, exact query, limitations, result count and selection decisions. No completed log exists here.

stages.forward: Stage 6 examines what the three identified publications substantiate and where their scope ends.
compare: Could someone reproduce your claimed search from the information you retain?
Are you distinguishing an example search string from a search you actually conducted?

stages.title: Evaluate, read, and extract sources
stages.where: The source set consists of two retrieval-learning experiments and one mixed-methods methodology article.
stages.changed: Each source receives a distinct evidence role and a boundary on its use.
reasoning: The 2006 experiment reports effects on retention under its own comparison conditions; it does not validate the present score scale.
The 2011 experiment addresses retrieval relative to concept mapping under its particular conditions, not six classroom interviews.
The 2004 methodological discussion supports combining approaches but cannot validate a particular set of codes or establish empirical integration quality.
stages.decision: Retain source metadata, identify study context and comparison, and quote or paraphrase only claims each publication supports.
stages.rejected: Reference authenticity is not evidence that the fictional scores, codes or interviews actually occurred.

notebook.sourceExtraction: MM-S01 and MM-S02 provide experimental retrieval background. MM-S03 provides mixed-methods rationale. All synthetic effects and quotations remain attributed exclusively to the example files.

stages.forward: The literature synthesis can now explain why these strands might be considered together without declaring an invented research gap.
compare: Is a methodological paper being asked to support an empirical finding?
Does your extraction record enough context to avoid misleading transfer between settings?

stages.title: Synthesize the literature and justify the study
stages.where: The fictional example has no new empirical contribution or documented literature search.
stages.changed: Its purpose is articulated as a methodological demonstration with a bounded educational context.
reasoning: Retrieval studies motivate attention to practice and retention, but this score table contains no concurrent comparison condition.
A reported study strategy can help readers consider how a student experienced a routine, without identifying the cause of the student's score difference.
A linked joint display makes those interpretive opportunities and uncertainties visible.
stages.decision: Justify the exemplar as an exercise in keeping quantitative change, short qualitative accounts and their integration distinguishable.
stages.rejected: Claiming that existing research overlooks this classroom or that the example resolves a debate would be unsupported.

notebook.rationale: This constructed teaching case demonstrates how a paired-score pattern may be read alongside linked interview snippets while maintaining uncertainty about mechanisms and generalisability.

stages.forward: Stage 8 develops a short source-grounded account that leads to the three-part question.
compare: Can you describe the study's contribution without inventing novelty?
Would the rationale remain accurate if the findings were different?

stages.title: Write the literature review
stages.where: The introduction needs to connect prior experimental evidence to the teaching demonstration without transferring experimental conclusions.
stages.changed: A short, connected literature narrative replaces a generic instruction to synthesise sources.
reasoning: Roediger and Karpicke (2006) tested retrieval against restudying and assessed retention at different delays.
Karpicke and Blunt (2011) examined retrieval alongside elaborative concept mapping, adding evidence that the type of study activity can influence later performance.
Johnson and Onwuegbuzie (2004) offer a framework for bringing numerical patterns and participant accounts into dialogue, provided the integration answers a substantive question.
stages.decision: Introduce the score strand as a descriptive paired comparison and the interview strand as a small set of linked accounts that may qualify its interpretation.
stages.rejected: The background papers should not be written as though they supply causal validation for this unobserved routine.

notebook.literatureReviewPlan: Retrieval studies provide experimental reasons to investigate what happens when students practise remembering. Their protocols and comparisons do not occur in this fictional one-group dataset. A mixed-methods reading therefore asks what the score pairs show and what six linked accounts add, while keeping the absence of a causal comparison explicit.

stages.forward: The design statement will identify the actual evidence available rather than assume a documented sequence of data collection.
compare: Do neighbouring source-based sentences build one explanation rather than merely name papers?
Have you separated findings reported by others from results generated in your own study?

stages.title: Choose the research design
stages.where: The fictional materials contain two score observations for 24 IDs and short interview excerpts for six of those IDs.
stages.changed: The design is described as a linked-strand mixed-methods teaching demonstration rather than an empirically documented convergent study.
reasoning: A within-student pre/post comparison measures change in recorded score values.
The interview file adds self-reported views from six selected IDs, and a joint display places these alongside the corresponding changes.
Collection timing, sampling decisions and researcher procedures are not documented, so a specific convergent or explanatory-sequential design cannot be verified.
stages.decision: Use a mixed-methods instructional structure with separate analyses followed by case-level integration; state that the one-group score component lacks a causal comparison.
stages.rejected: Labelling the files a fully executed convergent design would imply documented collection procedures that are absent.

notebook.claimBoundary: Describe paired differences and six linked fictional accounts. The integrated reading can suggest questions or tensions but cannot attribute score changes to retrieval practice.

stages.forward: Define the quantitative units, the excerpt units and the precise link between them.
compare: What specific moment in your design connects different types of evidence?
Does the design label promise procedures your records cannot document?

stages.title: Define constructs, variables, or evidence units
stages.where: Student IDs link numerical score pairs with the available interview excerpts.
stages.changed: The quantitative outcome and qualitative evidence units are defined without forcing them into a single variable scheme.
reasoning: Each quantitative case has a pre-score and post-score, with change calculated as post minus pre in score points.
Each qualitative case has one fictional excerpt and an initial interpretive code; no full transcript or interview guide is supplied.
The score scale, assessment comparability and teaching schedule are unspecified, so both score meaning and mechanisms require caution.
stages.decision: Treat the paired student as the quantitative analysis unit, the supplied excerpt as the qualitative evidence unit, and the common identifier as an integration link.
stages.rejected: Interview codes are not independent numeric outcomes, and score changes are not measures of students' stated experiences.

notebook.quantitative: 24 paired student-level score records. Change is post_score − pre_score and is expressed in unspecified score points.
notebook.qualitative: Six single excerpts with supplied initial codes. These are fictional accounts, not full interview transcripts.
notebook.integration: Join on student_id, then compare each excerpt's meaning with that student's numeric change without assuming causation.

stages.forward: Stage 11 examines what the available subset excludes and what an actual study would require ethically.
compare: Do your quantitative and qualitative measures refer to clearly defined units?
Can you trace every inferred construct to data rather than to a presumed protocol?

stages.title: Plan sampling, measurement, validity, and ethics
stages.where: Six interview IDs are included among the 24 score records; all six have positive changes.
stages.changed: The selection limitation becomes part of the research design rather than a minor afterthought.
reasoning: The six linked changes range from 9.1 to 17.1 points, with a mean of 13.93; the other 18 records average 6.95.
The only declining case, M11 at −4.6 points, has no interview excerpt.
The supplied files do not establish how interviews were chosen. It would be inaccurate to claim probability sampling, purposive selection criteria or thematic saturation.
stages.decision: Describe the six records as an available illustrative subset and avoid treating their perspectives as typical of all 24 cases.
stages.rejected: Inferring why the declining student performed differently is unsupported by the interview data.

notebook.sample: 24 fictional paired records; six linked interview excerpts (M03, M07, M09, M12, M18, M21). Selection criteria are unspecified.
notebook.ethics: For any real study, obtain suitable institutional approval and informed consent or assent where applicable, safeguard student records and limit grading-related pressure. No real participants are involved here.

stages.forward: Stage 12 specifies a transparent analysis sequence and matching fields for the joint display.
compare: Which experiences are missing from the subset you can analyse?
What real-world ethical duties would the fictional example require if conducted?

stages.title: Write the method and lock the data plan
stages.where: The quantitative CSV, excerpt CSV and summary JSON are kept as separate traceable sources.
stages.changed: A joint-display plan specifies exactly how strand-specific results will meet.
reasoning: First verify each post-minus-pre difference and summarise the 24 changes using paired statistics.
Then group the six existing initial codes provisionally, retaining the full wording of each corresponding excerpt.
Finally place IDs, score changes, excerpt evidence and cautious interpretive notes together. The absence of interview data for M11 must remain visible.
stages.decision: Create a six-row ID-linked joint display while also retaining a separate summary of the entire 24-student score distribution.
stages.rejected: A p-value cannot replace qualitative interpretation, and six one-sentence codes cannot establish a validated thematic analysis.

notebook.quantRow: student_id, pre_score, post_score, change_score; one row for each of 24 paired records.
notebook.qualCorpus: student_id, exact excerpt, initial_code; one entry for each of six fictional accounts.
notebook.integrationRule: Pair excerpts and score changes by identifier, describe agreement or tension and preserve the unknown causes of change.

stages.forward: Stage 13 checks all row-level arithmetic before the results are interpreted.
compare: Could another reader recreate your integration from the recorded identifiers?
What information would be lost by collapsing the qualitative strand into a numeric theme count?

stages.title: Collect or organize evidence
stages.where: All 24 score pairs are present, along with six linked fictional interview excerpts.
stages.changed: The score-change column is required to equal the recorded post-score minus pre-score for every ID.
reasoning: Initial inspection identified three transcription mismatches in change_score, for M02, M16 and M24; their corrected differences are 3.1, 9.9 and 16.4.
Using pre and post as the source of truth gives a mean change of 8.6958 points, consistent with the stored statistical output.
The interview excerpts are unchanged and can be linked to score rows. No transcripts, collection dates or verification of actual interview conduct exist.
stages.decision: Preserve the original pre/post pairs and six excerpts, correct the three derived-change cells, and document the corrections in the data audit.
stages.rejected: Adjusting the paired-test result to match an erroneous derived column would corrupt the demonstrated calculation.

notebook.dataSummary: 24 constructed pairs; 23 increases and one decrease. Corrected row differences yield mean change 8.6958 and paired-t 95% CI [6.1692, 11.2225]. Six linked fictional excerpts are available.

stages.forward: Stage 14 computes the paired statistics from the verified differences and examines how the six excerpts may be grouped.
compare: Do derived fields agree with the values from which they were calculated?
Can you preserve the original observations when correcting a formula-derived cell?

stages.title: Choose and justify the analysis
stages.where: The analysis uses 24 within-ID differences and six existing coded excerpts.
stages.changed: The numerical method, its inferential assumptions and the modest scope of qualitative grouping are described separately.
reasoning: For paired differences, the mean is 8.695833 points, their sample SD is 5.983636 and the standard error is 1.221405.
The paired statistic is t(23) = 7.119536, with two-sided p ≈ 2.98 × 10⁻⁷ and the conventional 95% paired-t interval [6.169166, 11.222501].

The six snippets support provisional groupings about noticing gaps, reconstructing ideas, feedback or study changes, and limitations of perceived transfer or repeated practice. They do not establish coded-theme reliability.
stages.decision: Describe the change distribution and paired-t teaching calculation, then present an ID-linked joint display with the original fictional quotations.
stages.rejected: Statistical significance cannot establish that the retrieval routine caused the observed difference, and thematic labels are not validated mechanisms.

notebook.analysisChoice: Compute post − pre for 24 IDs; report mean, SD, t with 23 df and paired-t interval. Group the six supplied codes cautiously, then integrate each excerpt with its linked change.

stages.forward: Stage 15 reports what each strand actually contains before discussing possible relationships.
compare: Do the test assumptions match the unit of analysis and the data available?
Are you calling exploratory code groupings 'themes' without acknowledging their limited evidence base?

stages.title: Write the Results or findings
stages.where: The quantitative strand covers 24 pairs; the qualitative strand consists of six excerpt-code records.
stages.changed: Results distinguish the overall score pattern, the supplied student accounts and the case-level comparison.
reasoning: Scores move from a mean of 66.175 to 74.871 points, with a mean paired change of 8.696; 23 differences are positive and M11 is −4.6.
M03 and M07 describe noticing explanation gaps and connecting ideas, whereas M12 and M21 mention using feedback or retrieval in their preparation.

M09 describes repetition as burdensome when content feels familiar, and M18 reports uncertainty about differently framed questions despite a higher quiz score. All six interview-linked cases improved, so the accounts cannot explain the declining case.
stages.decision: Report the paired interval [6.17, 11.22] as a conditional model calculation and use the six original excerpts to show both favourable and qualifying accounts.
stages.rejected: Do not describe a confidence interval as a causal effect range or imply the six excerpts represent all learner experiences.

notebook.result1: n = 24, mean change 8.6958 points, paired-t 95% CI [6.1692, 11.2225], t(23) = 7.1195; 23 increased and one declined. Six excerpts provide limited, linked interpretive evidence.

stages.forward: Stage 16 asks which alternative explanations and sampling restrictions constrain these results.
compare: Does each result originate from the corresponding file?
Are discrepant accounts and cases without interviews visible in your interpretation?

stages.title: Write the Discussion and limitations
stages.where: Neither the constructed score table nor the excerpts document a controlled intervention or independently verified interviews.
stages.changed: Limitations address both strands and the integration process, rather than adding a generic noncausal disclaimer.
reasoning: One-group change is compatible with practice, instruction, assessment differences, maturation or other factors; no concurrent comparison identifies a retrieval effect.

The two score instruments, scoring criteria, timing and independence across students are unspecified. A conventional paired-t interval therefore illustrates a model-based calculation, not a population estimate from an actual sample.

The six quotations are a selective, all-improving subset, while initial codes provide no full-transcript or independent-coder audit. They offer possible interpretations of experience but no proof of change mechanisms.
stages.decision: Keep the integrated claim at the level of a score pattern alongside contrasting fictional accounts and identify what a real study would need to test alternative explanations.
stages.rejected: Treating the interview descriptions as confirmation of score causation would conflate experience with effect identification.

notebook.limitations: All data are synthetic. There is no control group, intervention schedule, assessment-equivalence record, documented sampling scheme, full interviews or validated coding. Only six high-change cases have linked excerpts, and the sole declining case has none.

stages.forward: Stage 17 writes an abstract that communicates both evidence strands and these substantive limits.
compare: Does integration explain what the combined evidence adds without overclaiming?
Which alternative explanation would a sceptical reader expect you to address?

stages.title: Write the conclusion, abstract, title, and keywords
stages.where: The abstract must distinguish fictional observations from externally supported retrieval research.
stages.changed: The conclusion now identifies numerical change, the specific kinds of accounts available and the uncertainty they leave.
reasoning: The overall paired mean is positive, but the constructed example lacks a comparison group or documented protocol.
The six excerpts include perceived usefulness, feedback-related study decisions and reservations about repetition or unfamiliar questions.
The linked excerpt cases are all positive-change records; they cannot represent the full score distribution or identify a mechanism of improvement.
stages.decision: Conclude that the constructed dataset illustrates how linked evidence can deepen descriptive interpretation while leaving causal and representativeness questions unresolved.
stages.rejected: A concluding claim that retrieval practice reliably raises biology scores in classrooms is not warranted.

notebook.title: Retrieval Practice, Paired Biology Scores, and Student Accounts, a Synthetic Mixed-Methods Exemplar
notebook.abstract: This instructional mixed-methods example brings together 24 fictional paired biology scores and six fictional interview excerpts linked by student identifier. Mean score change was 8.70 points (paired-t 95% CI [6.17, 11.22]); 23 students had higher recorded scores and one had a lower score. The excerpts describe noticing gaps, reconstructing ideas and changing preparation, alongside concerns about repetition and unfamiliar questions. All six interview-linked records show increases, limiting their usefulness for interpreting the wider distribution. Without a control group, documented assessment equivalence or complete interviews, the integrated findings remain descriptive and illustrative.

stages.forward: The final stage audits source use, arithmetic, quotation fidelity and the limits of each inference.
compare: Does the abstract reflect the evidence actually reported rather than what the study hoped to show?
Are substantive limitations visible without overwhelming the example's instructional purpose?

stages.title: Citations, references, and final alignment audit
stages.where: The final source set contains 24 paired numerical rows, six exact fictional excerpts, a summary JSON and three genuine method or learning-science references.
stages.changed: The closing audit is an explicit evidence trail rather than a general claim of alignment.
reasoning: Recalculate all differences from the pre/post columns, including corrected M02, M16 and M24, and reproduce the paired-t interval and p-value.
Match each quotation to its student identifier and link its change to the corresponding quantitative row. Retain M11 as an un-interviewed negative-change case.
Confirm that Roediger and Karpicke (2006), Karpicke and Blunt (2011), and Johnson and Onwuegbuzie (2004) provide background or methodology, never fictional participant evidence.
stages.decision: Retain the synthetic status in the project, the standalone paper and the analysis record. Interpret integration as case-linked comparison, with no causal confirmation.
stages.rejected: The example cannot be presented as completed human-subjects research, a verified qualitative thematic study or a classroom intervention effectiveness estimate.

notebook.audit: 24 verified paired differences; 6 verbatim fictional excerpt records; 3 authenticated references; numerical paired-t replication; six linked joint-display rows; one un-interviewed decline; noncausal interpretation.

stages.forward: The eight-exemplar instructional bank can now be assessed as a whole before the Path Coach and Rescue banks receive their separate content audits.
compare: Can you trace each statistic, quote and interpretation to its precise source?
Would a reader understand which parts are published scholarship and which parts are constructed for teaching?
